Security.back: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information. Types: phishing (email), spear phishing (targeted), pretexting (fabricated scenario), baiting (USB drops), tailgating (following authorized person). Prevention: security awareness training, MFA, verify requests via separate channel.

Security.front: Explain the STRIDE threat model.
Security.back: Microsofts threat categorization: Spoofing (fake identity), Tampering (modify data), Repudiation (deny action), Information Disclosure (data leak), Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. Each maps to security control: AuthN, Integrity, Audit, Confidentiality, Availability, AuthZ.

Security.front: How does a Hardware Security Module (HSM) work?
Security.back: HSM is tamper-resistant hardware that safely generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys. Keys never leave HSM in plaintext. Accelerates cryptographic operations. FIPS 140-2/3 certified. Used for: PKI, code signing, database encryption (TDE), payment processing (PCI-HSM).

Security.front: What is OWASP Top 10?
Security.back: List of most critical web app security risks. 2021: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A04 Insecure Design, A05 Security Misconfiguration, A06 Vulnerable Components, A07 Auth Failures, A08 Software/Data Integrity, A09 Logging Failures, A10 SSRF.

Security.front: Explain how to secure a REST API.
Security.back: Use HTTPS always. Auth: OAuth2/OpenID Connect or API keys with scopes. Validate all inputs (schema, type, length). Rate limiting per user/IP. CORS strict configuration. No sensitive data in URLs. Audit logging. Response headers: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options.

Security.front: What is supply chain security?
Security.back: Vulnerabilities from third-party dependencies, compromised build tools, malicious packages. Mitigations: software bill of materials (SBOM), dependency scanning (Dependabot, Snyk), lock files (package-lock.json), pin versions, signed commits, reproducible builds, container image scanning.

Security.front: How does Docker container security work?
Security.back: Container isolation via kernel namespaces (cgroups, pid, net, mnt). Run as non-root user, read-only root filesystem, drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL), seccomp profiles, AppArmor/SELinux. Image scanning for vulnerabilities. Not root on host: user namespace remapping.

Security.front: Explain the difference between black-box and white-box testing.
Security.back: Black-box: tester has no internal knowledge, tests from user perspective (pen testing, fuzzing). White-box: full access to source code, architecture diagrams (code review, SAST). Grey-box: partial knowledge. Penetration tests often combine approaches.

Security.front: What is a DDoS mitigation strategy using rate limiting?
Security.back: Rate limit per IP, per user, per endpoint. Token bucket or sliding window. Application-layer: challenge (CAPTCHA, JS challenge) for suspicious traffic. Network-layer: blackhole/null route, BGP Flowspec. CDN absorbs at edge. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic bursts.

Security.front: How does cryptographic signing work?
Security.back: Signer creates hash of message, encrypts hash with private key (signature). Verifier decrypts signature with public key, compares hash. Provides: authentication (signer identity), integrity (hash mismatch detects tampering), non-repudiation. Used in JWTs, software signing, blockchain.

Security.front: What is a session hijacking and prevention?
Security.back: Session hijacking: attacker steals session token to impersonate user. Methods: XSS (steal cookie), network sniffing (unencrypted), session fixation. Prevention: HTTPS, httpOnly Secure SameSite cookies, regenerate session on auth, short session expiry, IP/user-agent binding.

Security.front: Explain the concept of secure coding practices.
Security.back: Input validation (whitelist over blacklist), output encoding, parameterized queries, least privilege, secure defaults, defense in depth, fail securely, don't trust user input, avoid security by obscurity, principle of complete mediation (check auth on every request).

Security.front: What is a CRLF injection attack?
Security.back:
Carriage Return Line Feed injection: attacker injects 
 sequences into HTTP headers or logs. Can lead to HTTP response splitting, log injection. Prevention: validate/encode newlines in input, use libraries that properly handle headers, never include user input directly in headers.

Security.front: How does a secure cookie configuration work?
Security.back: Flags: Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (not accessible via JS), SameSite (Lax/Strict prevents CSRF), Domain/Path scope, Expires/Max-Age. Partytioned (CHIPS) for embedded contexts. __Host- prefix enforces Secure + Path=/. __Secure- prefix requires Secure.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a SIEM system.
Security.back: Security Information and Event Management: aggregates logs from multiple sources, correlates events, generates alerts. Core: log collection (syslog, agent), normalization, correlation rules, dashboards, incident response. Popular: Splunk, ELK Stack, Azure Sentinel, QRadar, Wazuh (open source).

Security.front: What is the difference between MFA and 2FA?
Security.back: 2FA (Two-Factor): exactly two factors from: something you know (password), have (phone/token), are (biometric). MFA (Multi-Factor): two or more factors. MFA is superset of 2FA. Common: TOTP (Google Authenticator), SMS codes (less secure), push notifications, hardware keys (WebAuthn).

Security.front: What is a covert channel?
Security.back: Covert channel: unintended communication path not designed for data transfer. Storage channel: modifies shared resource (file existence). Timing channel: modulates timing of events. Used by malware for exfiltration. Prevention: resource isolation, noise injection, audit.

Security.front: How does API key rotation work?
Security.back: Generate new key, deploy to clients with grace period, support both old and new keys during transition, revoke old key after migration. Automatic rotation via secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault). Webhooks notify clients of upcoming expiration.

Security.front: What is the difference between RBAC and ABAC?
Security.back: RBAC (Role-Based): permissions assigned to roles, users assigned to roles. Simple but coarse. ABAC (Attribute-Based): policies evaluate user/object/environment attributes. Fine-grained, context-aware (time, location). ABAC more flexible but complex. NIST recommends ABAC for modern systems.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a blockchain security.
Security.back: Blockchain: tamper-evident distributed ledger. Security: hash chain (each block contains prev block hash), consensus (PoW, PoBFT), PKI for identities. Attacks: 51% attack (majority hash power), double-spend, smart contract bugs. Not immutable in practice (forks, rollbacks).

Security.front: How does a SQL injection test work?
Security.back: Tester injects: single quote (') to break string, 1=1 for tautology, UNION for data extraction, time-based (WAITFOR DELAY) for blind injection. Automated with sqlmap. Prevention confirmed when parameterized queries block all injection attempts.

Security.front: What is a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) vulnerability?
Security.back: CORS relaxes same-origin policy. Misconfiguration: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * allows any site to read response. Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with wildcard origin allows credential theft. Prevention: specific origins only, validate Origin header, avoid credentials with wildcard.

Security.front: Explain the concept of code signing.
Security.back: Code signing: developer signs code with private key, users verify with public key. Ensures integrity and authenticity. Platforms: macOS (notarization), Windows (Authenticode), Android (APK signing), iOS. EV code signing certs provide stronger identity verification.

Security.front: How does a VPN work?
Security.back: VPN encrypts traffic between client and VPN server, tunneling through public internet. Protocols: WireGuard (modern, fast), OpenVPN (mature, configurable), IPsec (enterprise). Split tunneling: only specific traffic via VPN. Full tunnel: all traffic via VPN.

Security.front: What is a session fixation attack?
Security.back: Session fixation: attacker sets user session ID before login. After user authenticates, attacker uses known session ID to access account. Prevention: regenerate session ID on successful login, reject URL-based session IDs, short session timeouts.

Security.front: How does a security code review differ from penetration testing?
Security.back: Code review: white-box, examines source code for vulnerabilities (SAST, manual). Catches issues early, lower cost. Pen testing: black-box/grey-box, tests running application. Finds runtime/configuration issues. Both needed for comprehensive security. Code review finds ~50% of issues.

Security.front: What is the principle of secure defaults?
Security.back: System should be secure by default: minimal features enabled, strongest encryption default, no debug mode in production, secure configuration out-of-box. Users should explicitly enable less secure options. OWASP: fail securely (deny access on error).

Security.front: Explain HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS).
Security.back: HSTS header tells browser to always use HTTPS for domain. max-age (seconds), includeSubDomains, preload. Prevents SSL stripping attacks. Once seen, browser refuses HTTP connections. Preload list hardcodes HSTS for major sites in browser source.

Security.front: How does a security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) work?
Security.back: SOAR integrates security tools, automates incident response. Playbooks: predefined response workflows (isolate host, block IP, generate ticket). Connects SIEM, ticketing, threat intel, endpoint protection. Reduces response time from hours to minutes.

Security.front: What is the difference between encoding, encryption, and hashing?
Security.back: Encoding: reversible format transform (Base64, URL encoding). No secret. Encryption: reversible with key, provides confidentiality. Hashing: one-way, fixed size, provides integrity. Encoding is not security. Encryption protects data. Hashing verifies integrity.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a security information sharing (STIX/TAXII).
Security.back: STIX (Structured Threat Information Expression): standard for describing threat intelligence (indicators, campaigns, attack patterns). TAXII (Trusted Automated Exchange): protocol for sharing STIX data. Used by threat intelligence platforms. Machine-readable threat sharing.

Security.front: How does a database encryption at rest work?
Security.back: TDE (Transparent Data Encryption): encrypts data files at OS/DB level. AES-256. Keys: DEK (Data Encryption Key) encrypted by KEK (Key Encryption Key). Key stored in HSM or KMS. Minimal performance impact (5-10%). Protects against storage theft, backup compromise.

Security.front: What is clickjacking?
Security.back: Clickjacking: attacker overlays transparent iframe on legitimate site, tricking user into clicking hidden buttons. Prevention: X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN, CSP frame-ancestors directive, frame-busting JavaScript (conditional). Common in social media like attacks.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a security key (U2F).
Security.back: U2F (Universal 2nd Factor): hardware token for second factor auth. Uses public key cryptography. User presses button to authorize. Phishing-resistant (origin bound). Works with WebAuthn. YubiKey popular hardware. No shared secrets, no server compromise risk.

Security.front: How does a application security testing (AST) pipeline work?
Security.back: SAST in IDE/commit stage, SCA (dependency scan) in build, DAST in staging, penetration testing pre-release. Results fed to defect tracking. Security champions review findings. Gate: critical/high findings block deployment. Continuous security validation.

Security.front: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
Security.back: Vulnerability: weakness in system that can be exploited (CVE). Exploit: code/technique that takes advantage of vulnerability. CVSS score measures severity. Zero-day: vulnerability without available patch. Exploit kits automate exploitation of multiple vulnerabilities.

Security.front: What is the difference between a covert channel and an overt channel?
Security.back: Covert channel: unintended communication path (storage/timing). Overt channel: legitimate communication path. Covert channels used for data exfiltration by malware. Detection: statistical analysis of resource usage, timing patterns. Prevention: resource isolation, noise injection.

Security.front: Explain the concept of API key rotation strategies.
Security.back: Rotate keys periodically (30-90 days). Phased rotation: generate new key, support both keys during transition, retire old key. Automatic rotation via secrets manager. Zero-downtime rotation requires client retry logic. Webhook notifications for upcoming expiration.

Security.front: How does Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) differ from ABAC?
Security.back: RBAC: roles group permissions, users assigned roles. Simple, coarse. ABAC: attributes (user, resource, environment) evaluated against policies. Fine-grained, context-aware. ABAC more flexible: time-based, location-based. NIST recommends ABAC. Hybrid approaches common.

Security.front: What is the principle of defense in depth for network security?
Security.back: Multiple network security layers: edge firewall, DMZ, internal firewall, network segmentation (VLANs), IPS/IDS, NAC (Network Access Control), micro-segmentation (zero trust). Each layer provides protection if the previous is breached. Defense in breadth: diverse vendors.

Security.front: How does a blockchain maintain immutability?
Security.back: Each block contains hash of previous block forming a chain. Changing any block requires recomputing all subsequent hashes (computationally infeasible). Consensus mechanism (PoW, PoS) prevents rewriting history. Tamper evidence: any modification breaks chain.

Security.front: What is SQL injection testing methodology?
Security.back: Automated: sqlmap identifies and exploits SQLi. Manual: inject characters ('), time-based (WAITFOR/SLEEP), boolean-based (1=1/1=2), UNION extraction. Test all input vectors (GET, POST, headers, cookies). Verify parameterized queries prevent injection.

Security.front: Explain CORS misconfiguration vulnerabilities.
Security.back: CORS headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * allows any origin. With credentials (cookies), this leaks user data. Dynamic origin reflection (echoing Origin header) bypasses origin checks. Prevention: whitelist specific origins, avoid null origin, never use * with credentials.

Security.front: How does code signing ensure software integrity?
Security.back: Developer signs binary hash with private key. Users verify signature with public key and trust chain. Protects against: tampering, malware injection during distribution, man-in-the-middle. Platforms: Authenticode (Windows), notarization (macOS), APK signing (Android), GPG (Linux).

Security.front: What is a VPN and how does it protect traffic?
Security.back: VPN encrypts traffic between client and VPN gateway. Protocols: WireGuard (UDP, modern), OpenVPN (configurable, mature), IPsec (suite, complex). Split tunneling: only specific traffic via VPN. Full tunnel: all traffic. VPN protects against ISP snooping, public WiFi eavesdropping.

Security.front: What is session fixation and how to prevent it?
Security.back: Session fixation: attacker forces a known session ID on victim before login. After victim logs in, attacker uses same ID. Prevention: regenerate session ID on login, never accept session IDs from URL/query params, use random high-entropy IDs, invalidate old session on login.

Security.front: Explain secure code review best practices.
Security.back: Focus on: input validation, authentication/authorization logic, cryptographic implementations, error handling, session management, data exposure. Use automated SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL) + manual review. Checklist-driven. Rate issues: critical, high, medium, low. Remediation before merge.

Security.front: How does HSTS protect against SSL stripping?
Security.back: HSTS header (Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000) tells browser to only use HTTPS. Prevents SSL stripping attacks where attacker downgrades HTTPS to HTTP. Preload list: hardcoded HSTS in browser source. includeSubDomains extends protection.

Security.front: What is SOAR in cybersecurity?
Security.back: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response): automates incident response. Playbooks: predefined workflows (block IP, isolate host, create ticket). Integrates SIEM, EDR, threat intel, ticketing systems. Reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Respond) from hours to minutes.

Security.front: Explain the difference between encoding and encryption.
Security.back: Encoding: transforms data for usability (Base64, URL escape). Reversible without key. Encryption: transforms for confidentiality (AES, RSA). Requires key to reverse. Hashing: one-way, integrity verification. Encoding is not security. Encryption protects data at rest/in transit.

Security.front: What is STIX/TAXII for threat intelligence?
Security.back: STIX (Structured Threat Information Expression): standardized language for threat intel (indicators, TTPs, campaigns). TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange): protocol for sharing STIX data. Used by ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers). Machine-readable, automated intel sharing.

Security.front: How does TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) work?
Security.back: TDE encrypts database files at rest. Data encrypted when written to disk, decrypted when read. Key hierarchy: DEK (Data Encryption Key) encrypts data, KEK (Key Encryption Key) encrypts DEK. KEK stored in HSM/KMS. No application changes needed. Performance impact: 3-8%.

Security.front: What is clickjacking and how to prevent it?
Security.back: Clickjacking: transparent overlay tricks user into clicking hidden buttons/links. Prevention: X-Frame-Options (DENY/SAMEORIGIN), CSP frame-ancestors directive, JavaScript frame-busting (window.top !== window.self). Social media: Like-jacking, tweet-jacking.

Security.front: Explain U2F security keys for phishing-resistant auth.
Security.back: U2F (Universal 2nd Factor): hardware token using public key crypto. Origin-bound: key tied to domain, prevents phishing. Challenge-response: browser sends challenge, token signs with private key, server verifies. WebAuthn standard. No shared secrets; server compromise doesn't expose keys.

Security.front: How does DAST differ from SAST in application security?
Security.back: DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): tests running application externally (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite). Finds runtime issues (auth, config). SAST (Static): scans source code (SonarQube, Semgrep). Finds code-level issues (injection, crypto). DAST later in SDLC, fewer false positives.

Security.front: What is CVE and CVSS?
Security.back: CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures): standardized identifier for known vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-12345). CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System): severity score (0-10) based on exploitability, impact, complexity. NVD (National Vulnerability Database) maintains. V3.1: Base, Temporal, Environmental metrics.

Security.front: How does a password manager work securely?
Security.back: Master password derives encryption key (PBKDF2/Argon2). Vault encrypted with derived key (AES-256). Vault stored on device/server. Zero-knowledge: provider can't access passwords. Browser autofill via injected JavaScript. TOTP and passkey support. Breach monitoring: check passwords against known breaches.

Security.front: What is the principle of fail-safe defaults?
Security.back: Access decisions default to deny. If permission check fails (error, misconfiguration), access is denied. Contrast with fail-open (access granted on error). OWASP: fail securely = deny on exceptions. Example: missing auth middleware should reject, not allow.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a bastion host.
Security.back: Bastion host: hardened server providing secure access to private network. Single entry point for SSH/RDP. Access logs audited. Hardened: minimal services, MFA required, SSH key-only auth, IP whitelisted. Jump box architecture. Session recording for compliance.

Security.front: What is DNS security (DNSSEC)?
Security.back: DNSSEC: adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records. Validates response authenticity (no spoofing). RRSIG: signature record. DNSKEY: public key. DS: delegation signer. Chain of trust from root zone. Solves: cache poisoning, man-in-the-middle DNS. Adoption: ~35% of zones.

Security.front: How does email security (DMARC/DKIM/SPF) work?
Security.back: SPF: list of authorized sending IPs. DKIM: cryptographic signature on email headers (selector._domainkey). DMARC: policy for SPF/DKIM alignment (p=quarantine/reject). Prevents email spoofing, phishing. BIMI: brand logo in email inbox. Aggregate reporting (rua) for visibility.

Security.front: What is the NSA/CSS top 10 security mitigations?
Security.back: Priorities: 1) Update/upgrade software, 2) Application whitelisting, 3) Implement least privilege, 4) Restrict administrative privileges, 5) Install and update anti-malware, 6) Network segmentation, 7) Multi-factor authentication, 8) Data backup, 9) User training, 10) Incident response capability.

Security.front: Explain infrastructure security in cloud (AWS shared responsibility).
Security.back: AWS responsible: security OF cloud (physical, hypervisor, network). Customer responsible: security IN cloud (OS, app, data, IAM, encryption). Shared: platform services (RDS: AWS secures DB engine, customer secures data/config). IAM policies define boundaries.

Security.front: How does a security incident response plan work?
Security.back: Phases: Preparation (tools, playbooks, team), Detection/Identification (SIEM alert, user report), Containment (isolate host, disable account), Eradication (remove malware, patch), Recovery (restore from clean backup), Lessons Learned (postmortem, improve). NIST framework. IR team roles defined beforehand.

Security.front: What is the concept of non-repudiation?
Security.back: Non-repudiation: party cannot deny performing an action. Achieved via: digital signatures (signer's private key), audit logs (immutable), trusted timestamps (TSA), chain of custody. Legal requirement for contracts, financial transactions. PKI provides non-repudiation through signature verification.

Security.front: Explain the principle of complete mediation.
Security.back: Every access to every object must be checked for authorization. No caching of access decisions. No assumption that previous check suffices. Example: after URL rewrite, re-check authorization. Applies to: file access, API endpoints, database queries. Defense against confused deputy problem.

Security.front: What is a CSRF attack and how to prevent it?
Security.back: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a user into executing unwanted actions on a web app where they're authenticated. Prevent with anti-CSRF tokens (included in forms, validated server-side), SameSite cookies (Strict or Lax), and checking Origin/Referer headers. Modern frameworks include CSRF protection by default.

Testing.front: What is the difference between unit testing and integration testing?
Testing.back: Unit testing tests individual components in isolation (mocked dependencies). Fast, deterministic. Integration testing tests interactions between components (real DB, network). Slower but catches interface issues. Both needed: unit tests (~70%), integration tests (~20%), E2E (~10%).

Testing.front: How does a test pyramid work?
Testing.back: Test pyramid: UI/E2E tests (few, slow, brittle) at top, service/integration tests (moderate) in middle, unit tests (many, fast) at base. Opposite is ice-cream cone (too many E2E tests). Ideal ratio: 70/20/10. Keep tests at lowest possible level.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of mocking and stubbing.
Testing.back: Mock: pre-programmed object with expectations of method calls. Verifies behavior (was method called with right args?). Stub: provides canned answers. Focuses on state. Mock frameworks: unittest.mock (Python), Mockito (Java), Jest.fn (JS). Use mocks sparingly; prefer real objects.

Testing.front: What is test-driven development (TDD)?
Testing.back: TDD cycle: Red (write failing test) -> Green (write minimal code to pass) -> Refactor (improve code). Ensures test coverage, drives design. Benefits: fewer bugs, better API design, regression safety, living documentation. Drawback: perceived slower initial development.

Testing.front: How does continuous testing work in CI/CD?
Testing.back: Tests run on every commit/PR. Gate: failed tests block merge. Stages: lint -> unit tests -> integration tests -> security scan -> E2E. Parallel test execution for speed. Test impact analysis (only run tests for changed code). Tools: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI.

Testing.front: What is the difference between black-box and white-box testing in QA?
Testing.back: Black-box: tests based on specifications, no knowledge of internal code. Equivalent partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables. White-box: tests based on code structure. Statement, branch, path coverage. Gray-box: limited internal knowledge (DB schema, API contracts).

Testing.front: Explain the concept of code coverage.
Testing.back: Code coverage metrics: line/statement (every line executed), branch (every if/else taken), function (every function called), path (every possible path). Tools: coverage.py, JaCoCo, Istanbul. High coverage != bug-free. Focus on branch + path coverage for quality. Target: ~80% line, 70% branch.

Testing.front: How does a smoke test work?
Testing.back: Smoke test: minimal set of tests to verify basic system functionality (deployment succeeded, service starts, endpoints respond). Run first after deployment. If smoke fails, rollback immediately. Quick (< 5 min). Build verification test (BVT) in Microsoft terminology.

Testing.front: What is regression testing?
Testing.back: Retesting after changes to ensure existing functionality still works. Types: re-run all tests (comprehensive, slow), selective (impact analysis), automated regression suite. Essential for CI/CD. Flaky tests (non-deterministic) should be quarantined and fixed.

Testing.front: Explain the difference between verification and validation.
Testing.back: Verification: Are we building the product right? (correctness of implementation). Validation: Are we building the right product? (meets user needs). Verification: testing against specs. Validation: testing against requirements. Both needed for quality.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test plan?
Testing.back: Test plan: document outlining testing strategy: scope, objectives, resources, schedule, test environment, risk assessment, deliverables, exit criteria. Key sections: features to test, test levels (unit, integration, system), test types (functional, performance, security).

Testing.front: How does performance testing work?
Testing.back: Types: load testing (expected users), stress testing (beyond expected), spike testing (sudden increase), endurance testing (long duration), scalability testing (linearity). Metrics: response time (TP95/TP99), throughput (req/s), error rate, resource utilization. Tools: k6, Locust, Gatling.

Testing.front: What is A/B testing?
Testing.back: Show two versions (A and B) to different user segments. Measure which performs better on target metric (conversion rate, click-through). Requires: randomization, sufficient sample size, statistical significance (p < 0.05). Avoid: peeking at results early (early stopping bias).

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test fixture.
Testing.back: Test fixture: fixed state used as baseline for tests. Includes: test data, object creation, configuration. Setup methods: setUp (before each test), setUpClass (before all tests). TearDown for cleanup. Avoid shared mutable state between tests (test isolation).

Testing.front: What is the difference between acceptance testing and system testing?
Testing.back: System testing: testing complete integrated system against functional/technical requirements. Acceptance testing: testing by end users/business to accept system. User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Beta testing, Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT). System: does it work? Acceptance: does user accept it?

Testing.front: How does a test double work?
Testing.back: Test doubles: dummy (placeholder, no implementation), fake (working but simplified implementation, e.g., in-memory DB), stub (returns canned answers), spy (records calls), mock (expects specific calls). Use fake over mock when possible (test with real-like behavior).

Testing.front: What is the concept of property-based testing?
Testing.back: Property-based testing: define properties that should always hold, framework generates random inputs. Example: reversing a list twice gives original list. Tools: Hypothesis (Python), QuickCheck (Haskell), fast-check (JS). Finds edge cases humans miss. Complement example-based tests.

Testing.front: Explain the difference between white-box and black-box test case design.
Testing.back: White-box: design based on code structure (control flow graph, data flow). Coverage: statement, branch, condition, MC/DC. Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC) required for DO-178C (aviation). Black-box: equivalence partitioning (input classes), boundary values (edge cases), orthogonal arrays.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test harness?
Testing.back: Test harness: collection of software and test data to run automated tests. Components: test runner, test scripts, configuration, reporting. Orchestrates test execution, manages setup/teardown, aggregates results. pytest, JUnit, Mocha are test harnesses.

Testing.front: How does API testing differ from UI testing?
Testing.back: API testing: request-response validation, no UI. Faster, more stable, earlier in pipeline. Tests: status codes, response schema, business logic, error handling, auth. UI testing: verifies rendering, interactions, visual consistency. API tests more reliable, UI tests cover user experience.

Testing.front: What is the difference between frontend and backend testing?
Testing.back: Frontend: UI components (React Testing Library), visual regression (Playwright screenshots), accessibility (axe-core), browser compatibility. Backend: API contracts, database operations, business logic, auth, performance. Frontend testing more brittle due to DOM changes.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test report.
Testing.back: Test report: summary of test execution results. Includes: pass/fail counts, coverage metrics, execution time, failed test details (stack trace, logs), environment info, trends over builds. Formats: JUnit XML, HTML, Allure. Integrated into CI pipeline dashboards.

Testing.front: What is the role of quality assurance (QA) in data engineering?
Testing.back: Data QA: data quality tests (null checks, uniqueness, referential integrity, range checks), pipeline tests (row counts, schema validation), output tests (consistency with source). Tools: Great Expectations, dbt tests, Deequ. Data pipeline CI/CD includes data quality gates.

Testing.front: How does mutation testing work?
Testing.back: Mutation testing: introduce small changes (mutations) to code (change + to -, remove if condition). Good tests should catch (kill) mutations. Kill rate = percent of mutants detected. Tools: PIT (Java), Mutpy (Python), Stryker (JS). High mutation score indicates thorough tests.

Testing.front: What is the concept of boundary value analysis?
Testing.back: Test values at boundaries of equivalence partitions. If input 1-100, test 0, 1, 100, 101. Off-by-one errors common at boundaries. Also test within range (50). Valid boundaries + invalid boundaries. Worst-case: combine boundary values from multiple inputs.

Testing.front: Explain the difference between compile-time and runtime errors.
Testing.back: Compile-time: syntax errors, type errors (static typing), import resolution. Prevent compilation. Caught by compiler/interpreter before execution. Runtime: null pointer, division by zero, network timeout, out-of-memory. Caught by testing + error handling. Static typing reduces runtime errors.

Testing.front: What is a flaky test?
Testing.back: Flaky test: non-deterministic, passes/fails without code changes. Causes: timing/race conditions, test order dependencies, external services, random data, environment differences. Impact: erodes trust in test suite. Fix: quarantine flaky tests, prioritize fixing. Tools: de-flake via retries (temporary).

Testing.front: How does a contract test work?
Testing.back: Contract test: verifies service complies with provider/consumer contract (OpenAPI, GraphQL schema). Provider tests: API produces correct responses. Consumer tests: client handles provider responses correctly. Tools: Pact (consumer-driven contracts), Spring Cloud Contract. Microservice testing strategy.

Testing.front: What is the difference between integration and end-to-end tests?
Testing.back: Integration: test interactions between 2-3 components (service + DB, service + API). Run in CI. E2E: full system flow through all components (UI->API->DB->external service). Slower, brittle, expensive. Run selectively, typically post-deployment in staging.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test environment.
Testing.back: Test environment: setup where tests execute. Types: dev (local), CI (isolated per build), staging (mirrors production), production (monitoring, feature flags for verification). Environments should be as production-like as possible. Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) for environment consistency.

Testing.front: What is the role of assertions in testing?
Testing.back: Assertions: statements that verify a condition is true. If false, test fails. Types: assertEqual, assertTrue, assertRaises, assertGreater, assertIn. Custom assertion messages improve debuggability. Soft assertions (collect failures, report all at end) vs hard assertions (fail immediately).

Testing.front: How does a canary release testing work?
Testing.back: Deploy new version to small subset of users (canary group). Monitor metrics: error rate, latency, user behavior. Compare vs baseline (control group). If metrics degrade, rollback. If stable, gradually increase traffic percentage. Automated: observation period + rollback triggers.

Testing.front: What is a chaos engineering principle?
Testing.back: Chaos engineering: proactively inject failures to test system resilience. Principles: define steady state (normal metrics), hypothesize steady state continues, introduce variables (server failure, latency spikes), disprove hypothesis. Tools: Chaos Monkey (Netflix), Gremlin, Litmus. Start small (blast radius).

Testing.front: Explain the difference between negative and positive testing.
Testing.back: Positive testing: valid inputs, verify expected behavior. Negative testing: invalid inputs (nulls, out-of-range, wrong types), verify graceful error handling. Both required. Positive tests prove system works; negative tests prove system handles failures properly.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test oracle?
Testing.back: Test oracle: mechanism to determine expected behavior. Types: human oracle (manual inspection), executable specification (formal), regression oracle (compare to previous output), consistency oracle (properties must hold). Automated oracle reduces manual verification effort.

Testing.front: How does a data pipeline test differ from a software test?
Testing.back: Data tests: check quality (row count, schema, null %, value ranges), lineage tests (upstream -> downstream), freshness (recency of data), reconciliation (compare source/target). Software tests: verify logic, behavior, performance. Data tests often use sampling and statistical properties.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test case management system?
Testing.back: Track test case repository, test execution results, defect linkage. Features: test plans, test runs, requirements traceability, reporting. Tools: TestRail, Xray (Jira), Zephyr, qTest. Helps QA teams manage manual + automated tests. Metrics: pass rate, coverage, trend analysis.

Testing.front: How does a stress test differ from a load test?
Testing.back: Load test: expected user count, response time targets. Stress test: increasing load beyond expected until failure. Finds system limits and failure modes. Spike test: sudden rapid increase. Soak test: sustained load over long period. Each reveals different performance characteristics.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test suite?
Testing.back: Test suite: collection of test cases grouped logically (by module, feature, test type). Organize hierarchically: test file -> test class -> test method. Test tags/markers for selective execution (pytest.mark.smoke, @Tag(SLOW)). Suite-level setup/teardown.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of test isolation.
Testing.back: Each test should be independent: order-independent, no shared state, no global side effects. Use fresh fixtures per test (or per class if immutable). Clean up after tests. Isolation ensures tests can run in parallel and are debuggable. Shared mutable state causes flaky tests.

Testing.front: How does a behavioral test (BDD) work?
Testing.back: BDD: tests in natural language (Gherkin). Format: Given (initial context), When (action/event), Then (expected outcome). Tools: Cucumber, Behave (Python), SpecFlow. Collaboration between dev, QA, business. Scenarios executable and readable. Living documentation.

Testing.front: What is the difference between performance testing and load testing?
Testing.back: Performance testing is broader: measures speed, responsiveness, stability under various conditions. Includes load, stress, endurance, spike, scalability. Load testing specifically measures behavior under expected concurrent user count. Performance testing encompasses all.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a synthetic test.
Testing.back: Synthetic test: scripted transaction simulating user behavior on a schedule (every 5 min). Proactive monitoring. Types: availability check, transaction flow, API ping. Run from multiple locations. Tools: Checkly, Datadog Synthetic, Playwright. Catches issues before users report.

Testing.front: What is the role of test data management?
Testing.back: Managing test data: creation, refresh, masking, versioning. Challenges: GDPR/PII protection (data masking), data volume (representative subset), data freshness (prod-like), referential integrity. Approaches: clone production (anonymized), generate synthetic, copy from staging.

Testing.front: How does a recovery test work?
Testing.back: Recovery test: verify system restores correctly after failure. Test: kill process, disconnect network, corrupt file, power failure. Verify: automatic restart, data integrity, replication catch-up, no data loss. Disaster recovery testing (DR drill) for critical systems.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a golden test?
Testing.back: Golden/master test: capture known-good output (snapshot, screenshot) and compare against future runs. Differences flagged as failures. Common for: rendering (UI snapshots), file generation (PDF/image), API responses. Needs manual update when expected output changes. Version-controlled snapshots.

Testing.front: Explain the difference between a mock and a fake.
Testing.back: Mock: verifies interactions (was method called? with what args?). Generated by mocking framework. Fake: lightweight functional implementation (in-memory database). Used for real behavior. Prefer fake over mock for stable tests. Fakes require maintenance; mocks are auto-generated.

Testing.front: How does a risk-based testing approach work?
Testing.back: Prioritize tests based on failure impact + probability. High risk (core functionality, security) -> more testing. Low risk (rarely used features) -> less testing. Risk assessment by team. Resource allocation matches risk level. Effective for limited time/budget.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test charter in exploratory testing?
Testing.back: Test charter: mission for exploratory testing session. Includes: area to explore, techniques to use, timebox, resources, notes. Example: explore checkout flow for edge cases (30 min). Exploratory: simultaneous learning + testing + designing. Scripted + exploratory balance.

Testing.front: What is the role of a severity vs priority of a test failure?
Testing.back: Severity: impact on system (critical: data loss, major: feature broken, minor: cosmetic). Priority: urgency to fix (P1: fix immediately, P2: before next release, P3: low urgency). Severity doesn't determine priority (cosmetic bug in landing page = high priority).

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test double in Python?
Testing.back: Python test doubles: unittest.mock (built-in), pytest-mock, responses (HTTP stubs), moto (AWS mocking). Mock: from unittest.mock import Mock, patch. Mock objects track calls, return canned values. Patch replaces real objects during test. MagicMock for magic methods.

Testing.front: How does a visual regression test work?
Testing.back: Capture screenshots of UI components, compare to baseline images. Pixel-perfect or perceptual diff (pixelmatch, looks-same). Fail if diff > threshold. Tools: Percy (cloud), Applitools (AI-based), Playwright Screenshot. Needs baseline updates when design intentionally changes.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a test runner and a test framework?
Testing.back: Test runner: executes tests, discovers test files, reports results (pytest, unittest, nose). Test framework: set of conventions and tools for writing tests (assertions, fixtures, mocking, parameterization). pytest is both a runner and framework. JUnit is framework with runner (Surefire for Maven).

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test coverage report.
Testing.back: Report shows which code lines executed during tests. Formats: HTML (annotated source), XML (Cobertura/Jacoco), JSON. Branch coverage: each condition's branches. Conditional coverage: each condition's outcomes. CI integration: coverage thresholds enforce minimum coverage. Badges in README.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test trigger in CI/CD?
Testing.back: Test triggers: manual (developer request), automatic (push/PR), scheduled (nightly), event-driven (deployment, dependency update). Selective triggers: run full suite nightly, run smoke on deploy, run unit on push, run E2E on PR. Webhook-triggered tests from external systems.

Testing.front: How does a soak test work?
Testing.back: Soak/endurance test: sustain load over extended period (hours/days). Goals: detect memory leaks, resource exhaustion, connection pool leaks, disk full degradation, cache effectiveness. Monitor metrics over time. Gradual degradation pattern indicates issues. Baseline + compare across runs.

Testing.front: What is the concept of test parameterization?
Testing.back: Run same test with multiple input/expected-output combinations. pytest: @pytest.mark.parametrize. Avoids code duplication, increases coverage. Combine with fixtures. Generate combinations with product (itertools.product). Named parameters for readability. Edge cases in parameter sets.

Testing.front: How does a state transition test work?
Testing.back: Model system as state machine, test transitions between states. Coverage: all states visited, all transitions exercised, invalid transitions tested. Example: order states (created -> paid -> shipped -> delivered). Test each valid transition + invalid transitions (created -> shipped without payment).

Testing.front: What is the difference between a happy path and edge case?
Testing.back: Happy path: normal flow, expected inputs, successful execution. Edge case: extreme inputs (null, empty, max values), boundary conditions, error conditions, unusual system states. Happy path tests first; edge case tests for robustness. Both needed for comprehensive coverage.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test retry strategy.
Testing.back: Retry flaky tests to reduce false failures: retry N times with backoff (linear/exponential). First retry immediate, subsequent with delay. Quarantine if flaky beyond threshold. Retry counts: 1-3 max. Conditional retry: only retry on specific exceptions (network timeout). pytest-rerunfailures plugin.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test architecture?
Testing.back: Test architecture: design of test automation framework. Layers: test definition (BDD/Gherkin), test logic (page objects, services), drivers (Selenium, API client), test data management. Patterns: Page Object Model (UI), Screenplay Pattern (tasks/abilities), Data-driven (external data). Maintainable tests.

Testing.front: How does a pairwise testing work?
Testing.back: Pairwise/all-pairs: test all combinations of parameters using orthogonal arrays. Reduces test count from exponential to quadratic. Most defects caused by single parameters or pair interactions (empirically). Tools: PICT (Microsoft), AllPairs (Python), Hexawise. Effective for configuration testing.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a continuous testing feedback loop?
Testing.back: Fast feedback: developer gets test results within minutes of commit. Pipeline stages: lint (< 1m), unit (< 5m), integration (< 15m), security scan, E2E (< 30m). Failure notification: Slack/email. Shorten feedback: test parallelization, optimize slow tests, move fast tests earlier. Fix Forward over Rollback.

Testing.front: How does a user acceptance test (UAT) work?
Testing.back: End users test system with real-world scenarios in staging-like environment. Verify business requirements met. Sign-off (formal acceptance) before production release. Types: alpha (internal users), beta (external users). UAT test scripts vs exploratory testing. Defect tracking during UAT.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test classification.
Testing.back: Test classification by: level (unit, integration, system, E2E), type (functional, non-functional), speed (fast, medium, slow), risk (smoke, regression), runtime (scheduled, on-demand), audience (developer, QA, business). Tags/markers enable selective execution. pytest -m 'not slow'.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a test scenario and test case?
Testing.back: Test scenario: high-level test idea/test condition (what to test). Test case: detailed steps, inputs, expected outputs, preconditions (how to test). Scenario -> multiple test cases. Example scenario: verify login functionality. Cases: valid credentials, wrong password, locked account.

Testing.front: How does a model-based testing work?
Testing.back: Create system model (state machine, decision table, sequence diagram), generate test cases automatically from model. Coverage: path, state, transition coverage. Tools: Spec Explorer (Microsoft), Conformiq, GraphWalker. Models needs validation. Good for complex logic, reduces manual test design.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test environment parity?
Testing.back: Production parity: test environments should match production as closely as possible (OS versions, middleware, network topology, data volume, scaling). Deviations cause environment-specific bugs (it works on staging but not production). Trade-off: cost vs fidelity. Containerization improves parity.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a bug and a defect?
Testing.back: Bug: error in code causing incorrect behavior. Defect: deviation from specification/requirement. Defect may not be a bug (incorrect requirement). Bug found during testing; defect could be in specs. Both: logged in tracking system, triaged, prioritized, fixed, verified.

Testing.front: How does a test impact analysis work?
Testing.back: Determine which tests to run based on code changes. Analyze dependencies: code coverage mapping (which tests exercise which code), call graph analysis. Run only impacted tests for faster feedback. Tools: Test Impact Analysis (Google), Microsoft Test Impact. Trade-off: coverage accuracy vs speed.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test data environment?
Testing.back: Dedicated environment for test data management. Types: static (fixed dataset), dynamic (fresh per test), on-demand (created at test time). Data sources: synthetic generation, anonymized production clone. Refresh frequency: per test, daily, weekly. Data versioning for reproducibility.

Testing.front: How does a load test with k6 work?
Testing.back: k6: JavaScript-based load testing tool. Script: define HTTP requests, check responses, thresholds. Options: vus (virtual users), duration, stages (ramp-up/steady/ramp-down). In-script: check, sleep, group. Built-in: metrics (http_req_duration, http_req_failed). CLI: k6 run script.js. Cloud execution.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test environment manager?
Testing.back: Provision, configure, maintain test environments. Ensure environment availability, consistency, and accuracy. Automate environment provisioning (Terraform, Ansible). Monitor environment health (service availability, data freshness). Coordinate environment usage across teams. Resolve environment issues.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test debt.
Testing.back: Analogous to technical debt: shortcuts in testing (missing tests, flaky tests, low coverage, manual tests not automated). Accumulates over time, reduces confidence, increases regression risk. Address: prioritize test improvements alongside feature work, automate critical paths, fix flaky tests.

Testing.front: What is a white-box penetration test?
Testing.back: Tester has full knowledge (source code, architecture diagrams, credentials). Tests internal security controls: authentication logic, session management, access control, business logic flaws, API security. More thorough than black-box. Finds deeper vulnerabilities.

Testing.front: How does a test of non-functional requirements work?
Testing.back: Non-functional: performance (speed, scalability), security, usability, reliability, availability, maintainability, portability. Test types: load/stress testing, security testing, chaos engineering, resilience testing, usability testing. Often requires specialized tools and environments.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a component test and a unit test?
Testing.back: Component test: tests a component/module in isolation (may include multiple classes/functions). Unit test: smallest testable unit (single function/method). Component tests may use real dependencies within module. Unit tests mock external dependencies.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test maturity model.
Testing.back: TMM (Test Maturity Model): levels 1-5. Level 1: Initial (ad-hoc testing). Level 2: Defined (test plans, process). Level 3: Integrated (testing throughout lifecycle). Level 4: Managed (measurement, quantitative). Level 5: Optimizing (continuous improvement, defect prevention).

Testing.front: How does a test of database procedures work?
Testing.back: Test stored procedures: verify logic (conditional, loop), check output (result sets, output params), edge cases (nulls, empty sets, duplicates), error handling (exceptions). Tools: tSQLt (SQL Server), utPLSQL (Oracle). For data pipelines: dbt test (singular + generic tests).

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test of idempotency?
Testing.back: Idempotency test: applying same operation multiple times produces same result. Important for APIs (PUT, DELETE), data pipelines (re-runs), message processing. Test: call endpoint N times, verify state identical after each call. Retry safety: no duplicate side effects.

Testing.front: How does a test of idempotency work for data pipelines?
Testing.back: Run pipeline twice with same input, verify output unchanged. Run pipeline after partial failure (checkpoint recovery). Test: exactly-once semantics, deduplication, upsert behavior. Idempotent pipeline enables safe retries. Partition/offset tracking for incremental jobs.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a smoke test and a sanity test?
Testing.back: Smoke test: verify critical functionality works (build acceptance). Broader, run on every build. Sanity test: focused verification that specific fixes/changes work. Narrower, run after fix/change. Smoke: build validation. Sanity: fix validation. Often used interchangeably.

Testing.front: Explain the concept of a test environment as a service.
Testing.back: Cloud-based test environments provisioned on demand. Benefits: scalability, isolation, production-like, cost-effective (pay-per-use), self-service. Tools: cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), containers (Kubernetes, Docker Compose), ephemeral environments (Preview apps, Review apps).

Testing.front: How does a test of event-driven systems work?
Testing.back: Event-driven testing: verify event emission, event format, event ordering, consumer processing, retry/dead-letter behavior. Test event schema evolution. Tools: testcontainers (Kafka, Pulsar), embedded brokers, contract testing (AsyncAPI, Pact). Event sourcing: test replay from event store.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test of idempotent APIs?
Testing.back: Idempotent API: repeated requests produce same result. HTTP methods: GET (safe), PUT (idempotent), DELETE (idempotent), POST (not idempotent unless design). Test: send same request multiple times, verify response and state unchanged. Idempotency key for retry safety.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test of at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery?
Testing.back: At-least-once: messages may be duplicated (consumer must deduplicate). Exactly-once: each message processed once. Test: insert duplicates, verify deduplication (idempotent consumer, transactional outbox, deduplication keys). Kafka exactly-once semantics via idempotent producer + transactional API.

Testing.front: How does a test network partition tolerance work?
Testing.back: Network partition: disconnect/reconnect nodes. Test cluster behavior: split-brain prevention (quorum), leader re-election, data consistency after partition heals. Tools: Jepsen (Clojure), Chaos Mesh, Toxiproxy (network simulation). Verify CP (consistency + partition tolerance) vs AP (availability).

Testing.front: What is the difference between a test of ACID and BASE?
Testing.back: ACID (SQL): Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Test: transaction rollback/recovery, concurrent transaction isolation (serializable), durable after crash. BASE (NoSQL): Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency. Test: eventual convergence, conflict resolution (CRDTs, last-write-wins).

Testing.front: How does a test of CRDTs work?
Testing.back: CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type): data structure that converges without central coordination. Types: state-based (merge), operation-based (broadcast). Test: concurrent updates from multiple nodes, partition + merge, convergence after gossip. Verify final state identical across replicas. Examples: Redis CRDTs.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test of schema evolution?
Testing.back: Schema evolution: forward (new reader reads old data) and backward (old reader reads new data) compatibility. Test: read data written by previous schema version, write data read by next version. Avro: reader/writer schemas match via schema registry. Protobuf: field numbers, optional fields, reserved.

Testing.front: How does a test of a message queue work?
Testing.back: Test: message ordering (FIFO), delivery guarantees (at-least-once, exactly-once), retries + dead-letter queue, throughput under load (bytes/sec, msgs/sec), latency distribution, durability (broker crash recovery), consumer group rebalancing. Tools: Embedded Kafka (Testcontainers), RabbitMQ test harness.

Testing.front: What is the role of a test of a distributed database?
Testing.back: Test: consistency model (strong, eventual), replication lag, read-after-write consistency, partition tolerance (AP/CP trade-off), CAP theorem behavior. Tools: Jepsen for fault injection, TLA+ for model checking. Benchmark: YCSB (Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark) for performance comparison.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test of data quality for production data?
Testing.back: Production data quality tests: null rate, uniqueness rate, referential integrity, type validation, range checks (min, max, mean, stddev), freshness (data recency), volume (row count). Monitoring: Great Expectations, Deequ, dbt test, Soda. Alert on quality violations.

Testing.front: How does a test of an OLAP system work?
Testing.back: OLAP (columnar DBs like ClickHouse, Snowflake): test query performance (latency, throughput under concurrent queries), compaction/merge behavior, partition pruning correctness, materialized view freshness, data ingestion rate. Star schema: verify dimension/fact joins. Cache warm-up impact.

Testing.front: What is the difference between a test of a SQL vs NoSQL system?
Testing.back: SQL: schema enforcement, constraint validation, ACID transactions, join correctness, query optimizer behavior. NoSQL: schema flexibility (document/wide-column), consistency model, key design pattern, partition tolerance, secondary index behavior, aggregation pipeline (MongoDB).

Testing.front: How does a test of streaming system exactly-once work?
Testing.back: Exactly-once: producer sends and commits transaction, consumer reads committed messages. Test: kill producer mid-batch, restart consumer with same offset, verify no duplicates and no data loss. Kafka: idempotent producer + transactional API. Flink: checkpointing + exactly-once sink connectors.

Testing.front: What is the concept of a test of multi-tenancy isolation?
Testing.back: Test: tenant data isolation (tenant A cannot see tenant B data), resource isolation (noisy neighbor prevented), per-tenant configuration, tenant-specific schema/data separation. Row-level security (PostgreSQL RLS), schema-per-tenant, DB-per-tenant. Performance isolation under concurrent access.

Testing.front: How does a test of a distributed tracing system work?
Testing.back: Distributed tracing: instrument services with trace/span context propagation (W3C Trace Context, Zipkin B3). Test: trace completion (all spans emitted), latency breakdown per span, sampling correctness, propagation across async boundaries (Kafka, gRPC, HTTP). Tools: Jaeger, OpenTelemetry SDK.

Testing.front: What is the difference between canary and A/B testing?
Testing.back: Canary testing deploys a new version to a small subset of users to detect issues before full rollout. A/B testing compares two versions (A and B) to determine which performs better on a metric. Canary is about risk reduction; A/B is about optimization. Both require proper monitoring and rollback capability.

Testing.front: How do you test async code in Python?
Testing.back: Use pytest-asyncio with the @pytest.mark.asyncio decorator for async test functions. Use asyncio.run() or the event_loop fixture. Mock async functions with unittest.mock.AsyncMock. For web frameworks, use httpx.AsyncClient to test endpoints. Key: await all async calls and manage the event loop properly.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between DevOps and SRE?
DevOps.back: DevOps: cultural/philosophical movement combining dev + ops, CI/CD, automation, collaboration. SRE (Google): applying software engineering to operations (reliability, SLIs/SLOs/SLAs, error budgets, toil reduction). SRE implements DevOps principles with quantitative reliability targets.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of Infrastructure as Code (IaC).
DevOps.back: IaC: managing infrastructure through configuration files (declarative/imperative). Declarative: desired state (Terraform, CloudFormation). Imperative: step-by-step (Ansible, Pulumi). Benefits: version control, reproducibility, automation, self-documentation. State management: remote state (S3, Terraform Cloud).

DevOps.front: How does a CI/CD pipeline work?
DevOps.back: CI: automatically build and test on every commit. CD: automatically deploy to environments. Stages: source -> build -> test (unit, integration, security) -> deploy (staging) -> E2E test -> deploy (production). Tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI. Gates at each stage.

DevOps.front: What is containerization and how does Docker work?
DevOps.back: Containerization: package application + dependencies into isolated environment. Docker: images (read-only layers), containers (runnable instances). Dockerfile defines build steps. Container runtime (containerd). Registry (Docker Hub, ECR). Orchestration: Kubernetes, Docker Swarm.

DevOps.front: Explain the difference between Docker and virtual machines.
DevOps.back: Docker: shares host OS kernel, lightweight (MB), seconds to start, less isolation. VMs: full OS including kernel, heavy (GB), minutes to start, strong isolation (hypervisor). Containers for app-level isolation; VMs for tenant-level isolation. Both can coexist.

DevOps.front: How does Kubernetes orchestration work?
DevOps.back: K8s: manages containerized apps across node cluster. Pod (smallest unit), Service (stable endpoint), Deployment (desired state, rolling updates), ConfigMap/Secret (configuration). Control plane: API Server, Scheduler, Controller Manager, etcd. Worker: kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime.

DevOps.front: What is a Dockerfile and its best practices?
DevOps.back: Dockerfile: instructions to build image. Best practices: multi-stage builds (reduce size), use specific base tags (not latest), minimal layers (RUN apt update && ...), .dockerignore, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, LABEL metadata, distroless base images. FROM scratch for static binaries.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of blue-green deployment.
DevOps.back: Blue-green: two identical environments (blue=current, green=new). Switch traffic from blue to green when green is verified. Benefits: instant rollback (switch back), zero-downtime deployment. Requires: load balancer/routing, full infrastructure duplication. Database schema changes need backward compatibility.

DevOps.front: How does a rolling update work in Kubernetes?
DevOps.back: Rolling update: gradually replace pods with new version. maxSurge (extra pods during update), maxUnavailable (pods that can be down). K8s ensures desired pod count. Monitors rollout status. Rollback via kubectl rollout undo. Canary within rolling: percentage-based traffic.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a configuration management tool?
DevOps.back: Manage system configuration across servers declaratively. Tools: Ansible (agentless, SSH, YAML), Puppet (agent-master, DSL), Chef (Ruby DSL), SaltStack (agent-master, YAML). Use cases: OS hardening, package installation, file management, service configuration, secret deployment.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a service mesh.
DevOps.back: Service mesh: dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. Sidecar proxy (Envoy) intercepts traffic. Features: mTLS encryption, traffic routing (canary, blue-green), observability (metrics, tracing, logs), circuit breaking, retries, timeout. Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
DevOps.back: Horizontal: add more instances (scale out). Requires load balancer, stateless design. Limits: practically unlimited. Vertical: add more resources (scale up - CPU, RAM, storage). Limits: machine size ceiling. Cloud: auto-scaling groups (AWS ASG). Distributed systems prefer horizontal.

DevOps.front: How does a load balancer work?
DevOps.back: Distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers. Algorithms: round-robin, least connections, IP hash (sticky sessions), weighted. Layers: L4 (TCP/UDP transport), L7 (HTTP/HTTPS application). Health checks: active (periodic probes), passive (observe failures). Tools: NGINX, HAProxy, AWS ALB/NLB.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a reverse proxy and a forward proxy?
DevOps.back: Forward proxy: client-side, represents client to internet (bypass restrictions, anonymity). Reverse proxy: server-side, represents servers to clients (load balancing, caching, SSL termination, DDoS protection). NGINX and HAProxy are reverse proxies. Squid is forward proxy.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a distributed system CAP theorem.
DevOps.back: CAP: Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request gets response), Partition tolerance (system works despite network partitions). Pick 2. CP: sacrifice availability during partition (HBase, MongoDB). AP: sacrifice consistency (Cassandra, DynamoDB). CA: not possible in distributed systems.

DevOps.front: How does a service discovery mechanism work?
DevOps.back: Service discovery: services find each other by name. Client-side: client queries registry (Consul, Eureka, etcd) for endpoint. Server-side: load balancer routes to registered services. Kubernetes internal: DNS-based (service.namespace.svc.cluster.local). Health checks deregister unhealthy instances.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a health check in production?
DevOps.back: Health check: endpoint (GET /health) returning status. Types: liveness (is app alive?), readiness (can it serve traffic?), startup (has it started?). K8s: livenessProbe (restart if fails), readinessProbe (remove from Service if fails). Returns 200 OK or 503. Include dependency checks.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a canary deployment.
DevOps.back: Canary: deploy new version to small percentage of users (5-10%). Monitor metrics (error rate, latency, business KPIs). Compare vs baseline. If stable, gradually increase traffic (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%). Automated rollback if metrics degrade. Feature flags can implement canary.

DevOps.front: How does a GitOps workflow operate?
DevOps.back: GitOps: Git repository as single source of truth for infrastructure. Changes via PR (review, approve, merge). Operator reconciles cluster state with Git (ArgoCD, Flux). Drift detection: operator reverts manual changes. Benefits: audit trail, rollback via git revert, declarative, familiar workflow.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a daemon set and a deployment in K8s?
DevOps.back: DaemonSet: runs one pod per node (logging, monitoring, node agents). Deployment: runs desired number of pods, managed via ReplicaSet. DaemonSet updated via rolling update or recreate. Use cases: Fluentd (log collection), Prometheus Node Exporter, kube-proxy. StatelessSet vs StatefulSet for stateful apps.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a pod in Kubernetes.
DevOps.back: Pod: smallest deployable unit in K8s, one or more containers sharing network namespace, storage volumes, IP address. Containers in pod communicate via localhost. Pod lifecycle: Pending -> Running -> Succeeded/Failed. Pods are ephemeral. Managed by Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs.

DevOps.front: How does a container registry work?
DevOps.back: Store and distribute container images. Public: Docker Hub, GHCR. Private: ECR (AWS), GCR (GCP), ACR (Azure), Harbor (self-hosted). Features: image scanning, signing (Notary), immutability (tag), retention policies, replication (cross-region). Pull-through cache for internet-facing registries.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a secret manager?
DevOps.back: Securely store and manage secrets (API keys, passwords, certificates). Features: encryption at rest/in transit, access control (IAM), rotation, audit logging. Tools: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault. Integrations: K8s (CSI driver, sidecar injector).

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a Kubernetes namespace.
DevOps.back: Namespace: virtual cluster within K8s cluster. Isolates resources (pods, services, configmaps, secrets). Resource quotas (CPU/RAM limits per namespace). Network policies (restrict traffic between namespaces). RBAC per namespace. Default: default, kube-system, kube-public. Not for hard multi-tenancy.

DevOps.front: How does a horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) work?
DevOps.back: HPA automatically scales pod count based on metrics. Metrics: CPU utilization, memory utilization, custom metrics (requests per second), external metrics (queue length). Target utilization: 50-80%. Scale up: rapid (metrics spike). Scale down: cooldown period (5 min). Algorithm: desiredReplicas = currentReplicas * (currentMetric / targetMetric).

DevOps.front: What is the difference between Kubernetes and Docker Swarm?
DevOps.back: K8s: feature-rich, large ecosystem, steeper learning curve, auto-healing, auto-scaling, rolling updates, service mesh integration. Docker Swarm: simpler, docker-native, easier setup, limited features, smaller ecosystem. K8s standard for production; Swarm for simpler deployments.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a Kubernetes operator.
DevOps.back: Operator: application-specific controller extending K8s API. Automates operational tasks (provisioning, backup, scaling, recovery). Uses Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). Example: prometheus-operator manages Prometheus instances, elastic-operator manages ES clusters. Follows controller pattern (reconcile loop).

DevOps.front: How does a container network interface (CNI) work?
DevOps.back: CNI: pluggable networking for containers. Assigns IP to pod, attaches to network. Plugins: Calico (network policy, BGP), Flannel (overlay VXLAN), Weave, Cilium (eBPF-based). K8s network model: every pod gets unique IP, all pods can communicate without NAT. Network policies for segmentation.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a monitoring stack (Prometheus + Grafana)?
DevOps.back: Prometheus: time-series DB, pull-based metrics collection, PromQL query language, alerting (Alertmanager). Exporters: node_exporter (system), kube-state-metrics (K8s), application metrics (/metrics). Grafana: visualization dashboards, alert panels, multi-source (Prometheus, Loki, CloudWatch). On-call: PagerDuty, OpsGenie.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of observability (logs, metrics, traces).
DevOps.back: Three pillars: Logs (structured, searchable, ELK/Loki), Metrics (numerical time-series, Prometheus), Traces (request flow across services, Jaeger/Tempo). Correlation: trace ID in logs + metrics. High-cardinality (traces) vs low-cardinality (metrics). OpenTelemetry for unified instrumentation.

DevOps.front: How does structured logging work?
DevOps.back: Log in structured format (JSON) instead of free text. Fields: timestamp, level, logger, message, trace_id, service, environment, user_id, request_id. Structured querying: grep for field=value. Tools: structured (Python), winston (Node), logrus (Go). Best practice: machine-parseable, human-readable fallback.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between centralized and distributed logging?
DevOps.back: Centralized: all logs sent to central store (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch). Single query interface. Single point of failure. Distributed: logs stored per node, query across nodes. Tools: Loki (distributed, pull-based similar to Prometheus). Cloud: AWS CloudWatch Logs, GCP Cloud Logging. Retention policies.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a distributed tracing system.
DevOps.back: Trace: end-to-end request path across services. Span: single unit of work within trace (service-specific). Start time + duration + tags. Propagation: trace context via headers (W3C traceparent). Sampling: head-based (decide at root), tail-based (decide after completed). Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry.

DevOps.front: How does a chaos engineering platform work?
DevOps.back: Inject failures into production/staging. Experiment types: pod kill, network latency, packet loss, CPU stress, DNS failure, region outage. Hypothesis + steady state + blast radius controlled. Tools: Chaos Mesh (K8s), Litmus, Gremlin (SaaS). GameDays: scheduled chaos experiments with team.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a backup and disaster recovery strategy?
DevOps.back: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): max acceptable downtime. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): max acceptable data loss. Strategies: active-passive (standby, failover), active-active (multi-region, load balanced). Backups: full, incremental, differential. 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite. DR drills regularly.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of database migration tools.
DevOps.back: Manage schema changes version-controlled. Tools: Flyway (SQL-based, Java), Alembic (Python/SQLAlchemy), Liquibase (XML/YAML/JSON), Prisma Migrate (Node). Migration files: up (apply change) + down (rollback). Automatically run in CI/CD. Best practice: backward-compatible migrations (add column first, deploy code, remove column).

DevOps.front: How does a CI/CD pipeline for data pipelines differ?
DevOps.back: Data CI/CD: test data quality (Great Expectations), schema validation (Avro/Protobuf schema registry), data lineage tracking (OpenLineage, Marquez), feature store testing, model versioning (DVC, MLflow). Data pipeline testing: row counts, freshness, uniqueness. Data build tool (dbt) for SQL transformations.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a stateful and stateless application?
DevOps.back: Stateless: no saved state between requests (request handled independently). Easier to scale (horizontal), restart tolerant. Stateful: saves state (session, DB, in-memory). Needs sticky sessions or external state store (Redis, DB). K8s: Deployment for stateless, StatefulSet for stateful.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a container lifecycle hook.
DevOps.back: PostStart: runs after container starts (before CMD). Grace period for initialization. PreStop: runs before container terminates (for graceful shutdown). Blocking, must complete before SIGTERM. K8s handlers: exec, HTTP GET, TCP Socket. PreStop: drain connections, save state, close DB pool.

DevOps.front: How does a service mesh mutual TLS (mTLS) work?
DevOps.back: mTLS: both sides present certificates, mutual authentication. Service mesh sidecar (Envoy) manages certificate rotation automatically. mTLS between Envoy proxies, terminating TLS at sidecar. SPIFFE identity: unique identity for each service. Istio: PeerAuthentication policy. Zero-trust networking.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a container runtime?
DevOps.back: Container runtime runs containers: pulls images, manages container lifecycle, handles isolation. High-level: containerd (K8s default), CRI-O. Low-level: runc (OCI runtime spec). Docker uses containerd. K8s uses Container Runtime Interface (CRI) to support multiple runtimes.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a Kubernetes Ingress.
DevOps.back: Ingress: external HTTP/S routing to cluster services. Rules: host + path -> service. TLS termination (certificate). Ingress controller: NGINX Ingress, Traefik, HAProxy, AWS ALB Ingress Controller. Annotations: rewrite, cors, rate limit. Gateway API (v2) is replacing Ingress for advanced routing.

DevOps.front: How does a DNS resolution work in Kubernetes?
DevOps.back: Pod DNS: pod-ip.namespace.pod.cluster.local. Service DNS: service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Headless service: returns pod IPs. CoreDNS: cluster DNS server, deployed as Deployment. Resolves cluster domain (cluster.local). External DNS: syncs ingress services with cloud DNS (AWS Route53, GCP Cloud DNS).

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Docker volume and bind mount?
DevOps.back: Volume: managed by Docker, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/, named, persistent, backup via volume drivers. Bind mount: host directory mounted into container, file-based, relies on host filesystem. Volumes preferred: portable, managed, backup-friendly. tmpfs mount: in-memory, ephemeral.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a Kubernetes ConfigMap.
DevOps.back: ConfigMap: store non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs or files. Pod consumes via: environment variables, volume mount (file per key), command-line argument. Limitations: 1MB size, namespaced. Updates: if mounted as volume, config changes propagate (with delay). Not for secrets (use Secret).

DevOps.front: How does a GitOps tool (ArgoCD) work?
DevOps.back: ArgoCD: GitOps operator for K8s. Continuously monitors Git repo, syncs cluster state to Git state. Sync strategies: automated (auto-sync, auto-prune), manual. Sync waves: ordered resource application. Health checks: verify resources healthy. Rollback: revert Git commit. Web UI + CLI.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a liveness probe vs readiness probe?
DevOps.back: Liveness: is app healthy? If fails, K8s restarts container. Recovers from deadlock/panic. Readiness: can app serve traffic? If fails, removes from Service endpoints. Prevents sending requests to loading/overloaded app. Startup probe: for slow-starting apps, defers liveness/readiness checks.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s StatefulSet.
DevOps.back: StatefulSet: for stateful applications (ordered, unique pods). Pod identity: stable hostname (pod-0, pod-1). Ordered startup/teardown. Stable storage (PersistentVolumeClaim per pod). Use cases: databases, message brokers, distributed systems (ZooKeeper, Kafka). Rolling update order: reverse (pod-N to pod-0).

DevOps.front: How does a container security scanning work?
DevOps.back: Scan images for vulnerabilities (CVEs) in base images and dependencies. Tools: Trivy, Clair, Snyk, Docker Scout, Anchore. Scans: OS packages (apt, yum), language packages (pip, npm, gem), secrets check. In CI: fail build on critical/high. Runtime scanning: Falco (syscall behavior).

DevOps.front: How does a self-hosted runner vs GitHub-hosted runner work?
DevOps.back: GitHub-hosted: managed by GitHub, limited customization, per-minute billing. Self-hosted: own infrastructure, full control, no minute limits. Use cases: large runners, special OS/arch (ARM), GPU, network-isolated builds. Actions Runner Controller (ARC) for K8s self-hosted autoscaling.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a build cache.
DevOps.back: Build cache: reuse artifacts from previous builds to speed up CI. Docker: layer caching (cache-from, cache-to, BuildKit). Package manager cache: pip, npm, maven. Language-specific: ccache (C/C++), sccache (Rust), bazel remote cache. Invalidate cache on checksum change. Cloud cache: S3, GCS.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a monorepo and polyrepo?
DevOps.back: Monorepo: all code in single repo. Consistent tooling, atomic commits, cross-project refactoring. Challenges: scaling git, CI (build only changed projects). Tools: Bazel, Nx, Turborepo. Polyrepo: separate repos per project. Independent versioning, simpler access control. Overhead: cross-repo coordination.

DevOps.front: How does a blue/green database migration work?
DevOps.back: Phase 1: add new columns/tables (backward-compatible). Deploy blue/green. Phase 2: migrate data. Phase 3: remove old columns (separate deployment). Dual-write: write to both old and new columns during transition. Read new if available, fallback to old. Zero-downtime migration pattern.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a feature flag system.
DevOps.back: Feature flag: toggle feature on/off at runtime without deployment. Use cases: canary releases, A/B testing, kill switch, trunk-based development. Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash (open-source), Flagsmith. Best practice: consume flag values eagerly, clean up old flags, uniform flags (same value for same user).

DevOps.front: What is the role of a deployment strategy (recreate vs rolling vs blue-green)?
