DevOps.back: Recreate: stop all old version, start all new (downtime). Rolling: gradually replace instances (zero-downtime). Blue-green: switch traffic between two environments (instant rollback). Canary: percentage-based traffic shift (gradual, monitored). A/B testing: route based on user attributes.

DevOps.front: How does a Kubernetes pod security context work?
DevOps.back: Pod Security Context: runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, supplementalGroups, seLinuxOptions, seccompProfile, capabilities. Security: runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: drop ALL. Pod Security Standards: privileged, baseline, restricted.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a Kubernetes network policy.
DevOps.back: Network Policy: specifies how pods communicate. Default: allow all. Policy: ingress (incoming) + egress (outgoing) rules. Selectors: podSelector (target pods), namespaceSelector (target namespaces), ipBlock (CIDR). Calico extends with global network policies. Zero-trust network segmentation.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Docker image layer and cache?
DevOps.back: Docker image layer: result of each instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD). Layers cached, shared between builds. Cache: layer is reused if instruction and context unchanged. Invalidation: changed COPY file, changing base image tag. Multi-stage builds reduce layer count. Dockerfile order: less-frequent changes first.

DevOps.front: How does a container penetration testing work?
DevOps.back: Test container security: break out of container (kernel exploit, misconfigured capabilities), escape via mounted /var/run/docker.sock, exploit shared namespaces, check default credentials, image vulnerabilities. Defense: read-only root FS, drop all capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, distroless images.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a readiness gate in K8s?
DevOps.back: Readiness gate: custom condition for pod readiness (not just container ready). Example: pod is ready when sidecar proxy is initialized. Additional conditions added to pod.status.conditions. Readiness gate must be satisfied for pod to receive traffic. Used in service mesh (Istio: sidecar.istio.io/inject).

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s mutating vs validating webhook.
DevOps.back: MutatingWebhook: intercepts API requests, modifies resources (default values, sidecar injection). ValidatingWebhook: validates resources against custom rules, rejects if invalid. Admission controller stages: mutating -> validating. Examples: Istio sidecar injector (mutating), OPA Gatekeeper (validating).

DevOps.front: How does a CSI (Container Storage Interface) work?
DevOps.back: CSI: standard for exposing storage systems to containers. Drivers: EBS (AWS), PD (GCP), AzureDisk, NFS, Ceph, Portworx. Pod mounts PVC -> CSI driver provisions volume, attaches to node, mounts to pod. Dynamic provisioning: StorageClass creates PV automatically. Snapshot/restore API.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob in K8s?
DevOps.back: Job: runs one or more pods to completion. For batch processing. Parallelism (multiple pods), completions (success count). CronJob: creates Jobs on schedule (cron expression). Timezone support (v1.25+). Use cases: data backup, report generation, scheduled batch jobs. Retry limit, deadline.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s PriorityClass.
DevOps.back: PriorityClass: priority value for pods (higher = more important). Preemption: higher priority pods evict lower priority pods when resources insufficient. Cluster autoscaler: respects PriorityClass. Critical system pods have high priority. Admission: PreventPriorityValue. Use sparingly, document priority levels.

DevOps.front: How does a container garbage collection work?
DevOps.back: Remove unused images, containers, volumes. Docker: docker system prune, docker image prune. K8s: kubelet garbage collection (dead containers, unused images). Container runtime GC: periodically. Image retention: keep last N versions. Node-level: disk pressure triggers GC. Registry: tag-based retention policies.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a taint and toleration in K8s?
DevOps.back: Taint: node attribute that repels pods (node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure). Toleration: pod attribute allowing scheduling on tainted nodes. Use cases: dedicated nodes (GPU), dedicated system pods, node isolation. Effect: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (evict existing pods). Tolerations can have tolerationSeconds.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s ResourceQuota.
DevOps.back: ResourceQuota: CPU, memory, storage limits per namespace, count limits (pods, services, configmaps). Hard limit: maximum total resources. Scopes: BestEffort, NotBestEffort, Terminating, NotTerminating. LimitRange: default resource requests/limits per pod/container in namespace.

DevOps.front: How does a K8s cluster autoscaler work?
DevOps.back: Cluster autoscaler: adds/removes nodes based on pending pods. If pod unschedulable (insufficient resources), add node. If node underutilized (< 50% for > 10 min), remove node. Works with cloud auto-scaling groups (AWS ASG, GCP MIG, Azure VMSS). Respects PodDisruptionBudget, node-level taints.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a vertical pod autoscaler (VPA) and HPA?
DevOps.back: VPA: adjusts CPU/memory requests/limits of existing pods (recommender + updater + admission controller). Recommends based on historical usage. HPA: adjusts number of pods. VPA + HPA compatibility: VPA works on CPU/memory, HPA on custom metrics. Avoid using both on same metric.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB).
DevOps.back: PDB: limits number of voluntary disruptions (node drain, cluster upgrade). minAvailable: minimum pods that must remain available. maxUnavailable: maximum pods that can be unavailable. Used by: cluster autoscaler draining nodes, cluster upgrade (kubeadm upgrade). Protects service availability during maintenance.

DevOps.front: How does a K8s custom scheduler work?
DevOps.back: Extend/default scheduler with: predicates (node filtering), priorities (node scoring), extenders (external scheduler). Multiple schedulers: spec.schedulerName in pod. Co-scheduling: group pods scheduled together. Topology-aware scheduling: spread across zones/regions. Tools: volcano (batch), kube-batch (AI/ML).

DevOps.front: What is the role of an init container in K8s?
DevOps.back: Init container: runs before app containers start (sequentially). Used for: waiting for dependencies (DB ready), data initialization, permission setup, schema migration. Restart policy: always run to completion. Resource limits apply. Pod fails if init container fails without successful completion.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s ephemeral container.
DevOps.back: Ephemeral container: temporary container for debugging running pods. Not part of pod spec, not restarted, not replicated. Use: kubectl debug, troubleshooting. Limited capabilities (no ports, no resource requests). Shares pod namespace (network, PID). Useful for distroless containers with no shell.

DevOps.front: How does a container data persistence with PVC work?
DevOps.back: PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim): storage request by user. PV (PersistentVolume): storage provisioned by admin. Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (single node), ReadOnlyMany (multiple nodes, read-only), ReadWriteMany (multiple nodes, read-write). StorageClass: dynamic provisioning with specific provider. Reclaim policy: retain, delete, recycle.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet scaling behavior?
DevOps.back: Deployment: scale up/down unordered, any pod can serve traffic (stateless). StatefulSet: scale up sequentially (pod-0, pod-1...), scale down reverse order (pod-N...), each pod has stable identity. Scaling: StatefulSet requires manual or operator-based scaling for data rebalancing.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s Service (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer).
DevOps.back: ClusterIP: internal cluster IP, stable endpoint for pod group (default). NodePort: opens port on each node (30000-32767), traffic routed to ClusterIP service. LoadBalancer: provisions cloud load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP TCP/UDP Load Balancer), routes to NodePort. Ingress: layer 7 HTTP routing.

DevOps.front: How does a container networking model in K8s work?
DevOps.back: K8s networking model: every pod gets unique IP, all pods can communicate without NAT. Pods on same node: bridged. Pods across nodes: overlay (VXLAN, IPIP) or underlay (BGP/Calico). CNI plugins handle: IP assignment (DHCP, host-local), routing, network policy enforcement. Service: iptables/IPVS rules on each node.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a K8s Headless Service?
DevOps.back: Headless service (clusterIP: None): returns pod IPs directly (no load balancing). DNS returns A/AAAA records for each pod. StatefulSet uses headless service for pod DNS identity (pod-0.svc.namespace). Use cases: Kafka (client-side load balancing), MongoDB replica set discovery.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s static pod.
DevOps.back: Static pod: managed directly by kubelet on node (not via API server). YAML manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. Used for: control plane components (etcd, API server, scheduler, controller manager). Self-healing: kubelet restarts if fails. No DaemonSet/Deployment management.

DevOps.front: How does a container image signed verification work?
DevOps.back: Image signing: sign image digest with private key (Notary, Cosign). Image verification: before pulling, verify signature with public key. K8s admission: check signed images, reject unsigned. Policy: only allow images signed by trusted authorities. Cosign: part of Sigstore (OpenID + transparency log).

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Docker Compose and Kubernetes Dev environment?
DevOps.back: Docker Compose: single host, simpler networking, good for local dev. K8s dev (minikube, kind, k3d): full K8s features, multi-container, service mesh, network policies. Dev environments: Telepresence (intercept remote services), Skaffold (continuous dev), Tilt (visualization).

DevOps.front: How does a developer local K8s cluster (minikube, kind, k3d) work?
DevOps.back: Minikube: full K8s in VM, multi-node option. kind: K8s in Docker containers, fast startup, CI-friendly. k3d: Rancher K3s in Docker, lightweight. All provide: local cluster for testing, container registry, load balancer (metallb). Integration: docker-compose bridge, host volumes, ingress controller.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s custom resource (CRD).
DevOps.back: CRD (Custom Resource Definition): extend K8s API with custom resources. Define schema (OpenAPI v3), CRD controller watches for changes and reconciles. Examples: Prometheus (prometheuses.monitoring.coreos.com), Cert-Manager (certificates.cert-manager.io). CRDs enable K8s-native application management.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a Helm chart in K8s?
DevOps.back: Helm: package manager for K8s. Chart: collection of K8s YAML templates + values.yaml. Features: templating ({{ .Values.replicaCount }}), dependency management, versioning, rollback. Repositories: ArtifactHUB (centralized), OCI registry. Helmfile/Kustomize for environment-specific overlays.

DevOps.front: How does a K8s admission webhook security work?
DevOps.back: Admission webhook intercepts resource creation/update requests. Mutating: inject sidecars, set defaults. Validating: enforce policies (no privileged containers, specific base images). Secure: TLS between API server and webhook, caBundle verification. Webhook timeout (30s default), failure policy (Ignore/Fail).

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Dockerfile and a docker-compose.yml?
DevOps.back: Dockerfile: build-time instructions (how to build image). docker-compose.yml: run-time configuration (services, networks, volumes, environment). Compose defines multi-container application setup. Development vs production: Compose for local dev, K8s/ECS for production deployment.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a container image layer reuse efficiency.
DevOps.back: Efficient layering: order instructions from least to most frequently changing (base -> dependencies -> code). Multi-stage builds: separate build and runtime stages. BuildKit: concurrent builds, cache mounts (--mount=type=cache for pip/npm), inline cache. Layer size matters: minimize layer data per instruction.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a canary and a blue-green deployment?
DevOps.back: Blue-green: full environment switch, 100% traffic at once, requires full infrastructure duplication. Canary: gradual traffic shift, percentage-based, requires fine-grained traffic routing (service mesh, load balancer weight). Canary enables monitoring during rollout; blue-green enables instant rollback.

DevOps.front: How does a K8s endpoint slice work?
DevOps.back: EndpointSlice: scalable, partitioned view of Service endpoints (replacing Endpoints). Splits endpoints into smaller slices (max 100 per slice). Topology-aware routing: prefer same zone. Address types: IPv4, IPv6, FQDN. Managed by EndpointSlice controller. Better scalability for large clusters (10K+ pods).

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s topology spread constraints.
DevOps.back: Topology spread: enforce even distribution of pods across topology domains (zones, nodes, racks). maxSkew: maximum difference in count between domains. topologyKey: node label (topology.kubernetes.io/zone). whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule (hard), ScheduleAnyway (soft). Pod anti-affinity for avoiding colocation.

DevOps.front: How does a container resource management (CPU throttle) work?
DevOps.back: CPU: requested as cores (1 = 1000m). Limit: hard cap via CFS quota. Throttling: container exceeding CPU limit is throttled (delay scheduling). Request: guaranteed CPU. Burstable: request < limit. Best-effort: no request/limit. Node capacity: sum of all container requests must fit. Compressible resource.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a K8s SA (ServiceAccount)?
DevOps.back: ServiceAccount: identity for pod processes (not human). Default SA per namespace. Pod can use specific SA. SA token mounted as volume (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount). Used for API server authentication. Image pull secrets attached to SA. RBAC: roles bound to SA for authorization.

DevOps.front: How does a container network policy egress filtering work?
DevOps.back: Egress policy: restrict outgoing traffic from pods. Default: allow all. Policy: select pods, allow to specific CIDR blocks, namespaces, or pods. Use cases: prevent data exfiltration, restrict internet access for sensitive workloads. Calico: global network policies (not limited to namespace). Audit logging for violations.

DevOps.front: Explain the concept of a K8s cluster federation.
DevOps.back: Federation: manage multiple K8s clusters from single control plane (KubeFed). Distribute workloads, services across clusters/regions. Use cases: multi-region HA, disaster recovery, cloud burst, avoid vendor lock-in. Challenges: network latency, split-brain, CRDs not federated. Alternative: GitOps per cluster.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between a Docker entrypoint and command?
DevOps.back: ENTRYPOINT: fixed executable run at container start (not overridable by default). CMD: default arguments to entrypoint (overridable). Docker run arguments: override CMD but appended to ENTRYPOINT. Pattern: ENTRYPOINT to script, CMD for default args. Simplifies: ENTRYPOINT alone if no defaults needed.

DevOps.front: How does a K8s pod eviction work?
DevOps.back: Pod eviction: node pressure (memory, disk, PID) triggers kubelet to evict pods. Priority-based: BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed. QOS classes: Guaranteed (request=limit), Burstable (request<limit), BestEffort (no requests). Node conditions: DiskPressure, MemoryPressure, PIDPressure.

DevOps.front: What is the role of a K8s Mutating Admission Webhook for sidecars?
DevOps.back: Webhook intercepts Pod CREATE, adds sidecar container (Envoy, Vault agent). Based on labels/annotations (sidecar.istio.io/inject: 'true'). Patches pod spec with init container + sidecar. Must handle: sidecar already present, pod in kube-system, exclude certain namespaces. Fault tolerance: failure policy.

DevOps.front: How does a container health check customization work?
DevOps.back: Custom health check: periodSeconds (how often), initialDelaySeconds (delay before first check), timeoutSeconds (probe timeout), successThreshold (consecutive successes for ready), failureThreshold (consecutive failures for unhealthy). Tuning: balance between detection speed and false positives.

DevOps.front: What is the difference between StatefulSet and Deployment in Kubernetes?
DevOps.back: Deployment manages stateless pods with identical replicas, shared PVC, random scaling. StatefulSet manages stateful pods with unique identities (stable network IDs, persistent storage per pod), ordered scaling. Use Deployment for stateless apps (web servers). Use StatefulSet for databases, message queues, and any app requiring stable identity.

DevOps.front: Explain the difference between taints/tolerations and node affinity.
DevOps.back: Taints repel pods from nodes unless the pod has a matching toleration (node → pod: 'do not schedule here unless you tolerate'). Node affinity attracts pods to nodes based on labels (pod → node: 'I prefer to run here'). Taints are for node-level constraints (dedicated nodes, GPU nodes); affinity is for pod placement preferences and requirements.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Singleton pattern and when to use it?
Design Patterns.back: Singleton: ensures class has only one instance, provides global access point. Python: __new__ override or module-level instance. Use: logging, configuration, connection pools, caching. Avoid: hides dependencies (global state), hard to test (mocking). Dependency injection preferred over singleton for testability.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Factory pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Factory: creates objects without specifying exact class. Simple Factory: single function creating objects. Factory Method: subclass decides which class to instantiate. Abstract Factory: creates families of related objects. Use: when object creation logic is complex or varies by context.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Observer pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Observer: one-to-many dependency; when subject changes state, all observers notified. Python: built-in property + __setattr__, or custom Observable/Subject. Async: async observers via async callbacks. Use: event handling, UI updates, pub/sub systems (Redis pub/sub, Kafka). Alternative: signals (Django, Blinker).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Strategy pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Strategy: family of interchangeable algorithms encapsulated behind common interface. Context delegates to strategy. Open/Closed principle: add strategies without modifying context. Python: first-class functions can replace Strategy pattern (pass function as argument). Use: sorting strategies, compression, payment processors.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Decorator pattern (structural).
Design Patterns.back: Decorator: wraps object with additional behavior without modifying class. Python: decorators (functions wrapping functions), or class-based decorators (__call__). Use: logging, timing, caching, authentication, rate limiting. Compose multiple decorators. Also structural decorator pattern with same interface.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Adapter pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Adapter: converts interface of one class to interface expected by client. Class adapter (multiple inheritance) vs object adapter (composition). Use: integrate incompatible interfaces, legacy systems, third-party libraries. Python duck typing reduces need for adapter; wrapper class still useful.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Proxy pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Proxy: placeholder controlling access to another object. Types: virtual proxy (lazy initialization), protection proxy (access control), remote proxy (network stub), caching proxy. Python: __getattr__ delegation. Use: lazy loading (heavy resource), access logging, distributed systems (gRPC stub).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Command pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Command: encapsulates request as object. Components: Invoker (triggers command), Command (interface with execute), Receiver (performs action). Use: undo/redo (store command history), queue operations, macro recording. Python: partial functions can implement simple commands. GUI actions, job queues (Celery).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Template Method pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Template Method: defines algorithm skeleton in base class, steps implemented by subclasses. Hook methods: optional overridable steps. Hollywood principle: don't call us, we'll call you. Use: data processing pipelines (ETL steps), game AI, testing frameworks (setUp -> test -> tearDown).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Iterator pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Iterator: provides sequential access to elements without exposing underlying representation. Python: __iter__ (returns iterator) + __next__ (returns next element). Generator functions (yield) simplify iterators. Use: traversing collections, lazy evaluation, streaming data. Built-in: for loops use iterator protocol.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Composite pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Composite: tree structure where individual objects and compositions are treated uniformly. Component interface with common operations. Leaf (end object) and Composite (container of children). Use: file system (file/directory hierarchy), UI components, organizational charts, AST nodes.

Design Patterns.front: What is the State pattern?
Design Patterns.back: State: allows object to change behavior when internal state changes (state machine). Context holds current State object. Each state implements behavior for events. Transitions: state object decides next state. Use: order processing (new->paid->shipped), game character states, workflow engines.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Facade pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Facade: provides simplified interface to complex subsystem. Reduces coupling, hides complexity. Subsystems don't know facade exists. Use: wrapping complex libraries (ffmpeg, AWS SDK), simplifying API for common use cases. Python's __init__.py can serve as facade for module package.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Builder pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Builder: separates construction of complex object from its representation. Fluent interface (method chaining for readability). Director orchestrates building process (optional). Use: constructing objects with many optional parameters (PizzaBuilder, QueryBuilder, HTML builder). Python kwargs partially replaces.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Prototype pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Prototype: creates new objects by cloning existing instance. Python: copy.copy (shallow), copy.deepcopy (deep). Cloning avoids expensive creation. Use: when object creation is expensive (DB queries, complex setup), when many similar instances needed. Register prototypes for dynamic configuration.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Chain of Responsibility pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Chain of Responsibility: passes request along chain of handlers until one handles it. Each handler decides to handle or pass to next. Python: linked list of handlers with handle() method. Use: logging (severity levels), authentication middleware (OAuth, JWT, API key), validation pipelines.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Mediator pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Mediator: centralizes communication between objects (colleagues). Colleagues don't know each other directly. Reduces coupling, simplifies interactions. Use: chat rooms, GUI dialog (components communicate via dialog), air traffic control. Alternative: publish-subscribe (message broker).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Memento pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Memento: captures and externalizes object's internal state so it can be restored later. Originator (creates memento), Caretaker (stores mementos). Use: undo/redo, save points in games, checkpoint/rollback. Python: pickle/serialization for state persistence. Memory vs storage trade-off.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Visitor pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Visitor: separates algorithm from object structure. New operations added without modifying classes. Double dispatch: dynamically dispatches based on both visitor's and element's types. Use: AST processing (compilers), reporting, validation over heterogeneous structures. Python can use singledispatch.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Interpreter pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Interpreter: defines grammar for language, interprets sentences in that language. AST nodes represent grammar rules. Terminal expressions (literals) vs non-terminal (composite rules). Use: DSLs, regex engines, SQL parsers, configuration language parsers. Python's ast module for Python code parsing.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Repository pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Repository: mediates between domain and data mapping layers. Provides collection-like interface for accessing domain objects. Decouples business logic from data access. Use: complex queries, testability (mock repository), multiple data sources. Python: SQLAlchemy session can serve as repository pattern.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Data Mapper pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Data Mapper: separates in-memory objects from database. Maps between object properties and DB columns. Rows -> objects, objects -> rows. No persistence logic in domain objects. SQLAlchemy ORM implements data mapper. Active Record (Django ORM) combines domain and persistence logic.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Dependency Injection pattern.
Design Patterns.back: DI: passes dependencies into object (constructor, setter, or interface injection). Inversion of Control: framework manages dependencies. Benefits: loose coupling, testability (mock dependencies), flexibility. Python: simple argument injection, or frameworks (FastAPI Depends). Without DI: hard-coded dependencies.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Inversion of Control (IoC) principle?
Design Patterns.back: IoC: framework calls into application code (instead of application calling library). Hollywood principle: don't call us, we'll call you. DI is form of IoC. Event-driven programming, template method, service locator all IoC. Spring, FastAPI, Django use IoC for component wiring.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the ActiveRecord pattern.
Design Patterns.back: ActiveRecord: domain object is also responsible for persistence. Each DB row is object. Methods: save, update, delete, find. Django ORM, Ruby on Rails ActiveRecord. Simple but violates single-responsibility. Less coupling: Data Mapper (SQLAlchemy) separates concerns.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Object Pool pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Object Pool: reusable pool of objects (expensive to create/recycle). Borrow-return lifecycle. Thread safety: acquire/release with locking. Use: database connections (psycopg2 pool), thread pools (concurrent.futures), network connections. Pre-allocation vs lazy allocation. LRU cleanup of idle objects.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Lazy Loading pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Lazy loading: defer object initialization until needed. Types: lazy initialization (create on first access), virtual proxy (stand-in object), value holder (wrapper), ghost (partially loaded object). Use: expensive resources (DB queries, file reads), large collections. Python: @property lazy loading, descriptor protocol.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Service Locator pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Service Locator: central registry for services. Components request services from locator. Anti-pattern critique: hides dependencies, makes testing harder (global mutable reference). DI preferred. Use: legacy systems, dynamic service resolution, plugin architectures. Python: module-level dictionary of services.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Data Transfer Object (DTO) pattern?
Design Patterns.back: DTO: simple object carrying data between processes (network, service boundaries). No business logic. Serialized/deserialized (JSON, Protobuf, Avro). Python: dataclass, NamedTuple, Pydantic model. Use: API request/response, between microservices, avoid exposing internal entities.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the DAO (Data Access Object) pattern.
Design Patterns.back: DAO: abstracts persistence operations (CRUD) behind interface. Separate from business logic. Implementation per data source (SQL, NoSQL, file). Repository vs DAO: repository is domain-focused, DAO is data-focused. Python: DAO generic with SQLAlchemy session. Test: mock DAO interface.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Concrete Factory vs Abstract Factory differ?
Design Patterns.back: Simple Factory: single class (static method) returns product. Factory Method: inheritance-based, subclass creates product. Abstract Factory: interface for creating related families, implemented by concrete factories (Windows/Mac/Linux UI factories). Abstract Factory extends Factory Method with multiple products.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Bridge pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Bridge: decouples abstraction from implementation so both vary independently. Uses composition (has-a) instead of inheritance (is-a). Abstraction delegates to Implementor. Use: cross-platform graphics (Windows/DirectX vs Linux/Vulkan), device drivers, UI frameworks. Prevents class explosion (platform * feature).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Flyweight pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Flyweight: shares object state to minimize memory. Intrinsic (shared, immutable) vs extrinsic (context, passed in). Factory manages flyweight pool. Use: character rendering (shared glyph data), game particles (shared texture), thread-safe connections. Python: interning of small strings is flyweight pattern.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Null Object pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Null Object: replaces None/null checks with do-nothing object implementing same interface. No-op methods. Use: optional dependencies, default behaviors, eliminate conditionals. Python: object with __bool__ = False. Example: empty collection vs null in streaming data processing.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Model: business logic + data. View: presentation/UI. Controller: handles input, updates model, selects view. Django: Model-View-Template (MTV) variant. FastAPI + Jinja2: MVT. Separation of concerns: test model independently, swap views. Modern SPA: API (model) + frontend (view).

Design Patterns.front: How does the MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: MVVM: ViewModel exposes model data as observable properties for View binding. Two-way data binding: View changes automatically update ViewModel and vice versa. WPF, Angular, Vue, Knockout. ViewModel is state + commands for view. Test ViewModel independently of View (no UI dependency).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Difference between MVC and MVVM?
Design Patterns.back: MVC: Controller handles user input, updates Model, selects View. MVVM: ViewModel exposes data + commands via observable properties, View binds to them. MVVM has automatic two-way binding (less glue code). MVC more common for server-side (Django, Rails), MVVM for client-side (Angular, WPF).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Event Sourcing pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Event Sourcing: state represented as sequence of events. Current state = fold/reduce of events. Benefits: audit trail, temporal queries, rebuild state from scratch, event-driven architecture. Stores: EventStoreDB, Kafka. Challenges: schema evolution, event versioning, eventual consistency.

Design Patterns.front: What is the CQRS pattern?
Design Patterns.back: CQRS: separate read and write models. Command: mutates state (write). Query: retrieves state (read). Separate databases optimized per operation. Benefits: independent scaling, optimized read models (denormalized), write model enforces domain rules. Simple CQRS: separate service interfaces. Full CQRS + Event Sourcing.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Saga orchestration pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Saga: distributed transaction across microservices. Choreography: each service produces events triggering next service. Orchestration: central coordinator (orchestrator) tells services what to do. Compensating actions (undo) on failure. Use: order processing (create order -> reserve inventory -> charge payment -> ship order).

Design Patterns.front: How does the Outbox pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Outbox: transactional outbox table for reliable event publishing. In same DB transaction as business operation. Outbox reader/relay publishes events to message broker (CDC change data capture - Debezium, or polling). Guarantees: exactly-once delivery (no dual-write problem). Cancel outbox vs domain outbox.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Saga choreography pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Saga choreography: no central coordinator. Each service after action publishes event, next service listens and acts. Compensating events on failure. Pros: decentralized, simpler. Cons: hard to track, cyclic dependencies. Use: simpler workflows. Async communication via message broker (RabbitMQ, Kafka).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Circuit Breaker: prevents cascading failures by stopping calls to failing service. States: closed (normal, calls pass), open (failing, calls fail fast), half-open (test calls after timeout). Metrics: failure count/threshold, timeout. Recovery: after reset timeout, allow test calls. Tools: Hystrix, resilience4j, Python pybreaker.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Bulkhead pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Bulkhead: isolates resources into pools so failure in one pool doesn't cascade. Thread pools per service, connection pools per downstream. Fixed number of connections/threads per partition. Compartmentalization: ship hull analogy. Use: separate thread pools for different API endpoints, separate connection pools per DB.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Retry pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Retry: automatically retry failed operations (transient faults). Wait strategies: fixed, incremental, exponential backoff, jitter. Max retries + timeout. Idempotency required. Use: network calls, DB operations, distributed systems. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents thundering herd.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Throttling pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Throttling: rate limit requests to protect system. Strategies: token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window, fixed window. Levels: per-user, per-IP, per-endpoint. Response: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Queuing: buffer requests instead of rejecting.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Strangler Fig pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Strangler Fig: gradually replace legacy system with new system. Intercept calls to legacy, route to new functionality incrementally. Eventually legacy system strangled. Use: monolith to microservices migration. Proxy/gateway routes by URL path/user ID. Modernize piece by piece, production proven.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Sidecar pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Sidecar: deploy helper component alongside main application (same pod). Shared lifecycle, network, storage. Use: logging, monitoring, proxy, sync, TLS termination. Service mesh uses sidecar proxies (Envoy). Vault agent sidecar for secret rotation. Offload concerns from main application container.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Ambassador pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Ambassador: proxy service sitting in front of main service. Handles cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, caching, circuit breaking, retries. Sidecar vs Ambassador: Ambassador acts as intermediary, often outside application process. K8s: ambassador pattern as API Gateway.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Adapter (microservices) pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Adapter: translates between incompatible service interfaces. Protocol conversion (SOAP to REST), data format transformation (XML to JSON), version translation. Use: integrating legacy services, API versioning, vendor-specific adapters. Implemented as separate microservice (API gateway adapter).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Backends for Frontends (BFF) pattern?
Design Patterns.back: BFF: separate backend per client type (mobile, web, desktop). Each BFF optimized for specific client needs (payload size, data format, API design). Avoids generic API that serves all clients poorly. Co-located with client team. Simplifies frontend, backend tailored to use case.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the API Gateway pattern.
Design Patterns.back: API Gateway: single entry point for multiple microservices. Routing, authentication, rate limiting, caching, request/response transformation, aggregation. Cross-cutting concerns handled centrally. Tools: Kong, NGINX Plus, AWS API Gateway, Zuul. Backend for Frontends is variation (per-client gateway).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Gateway Aggregation pattern?
Design Patterns.back: API Gateway aggregates responses from multiple services into single response. Request -> gateway -> parallel calls to services -> combined response. Reduces client round trips. Use: dashboard that needs data from multiple services. Risk: gateway becomes bottleneck. Use async I/O for parallel calls.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Gateway Routing pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Route requests to appropriate service based on path, header, or query parameter. Example: /users/* -> user-service, /orders/* -> order-service. Load balancing across service instances. Path-based routing in ingress controllers. Content-based routing (request type/header). Blue-green via routing rules.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Choreography pattern in microservices?
Design Patterns.back: Choreography: each service makes local decisions and publishes events. Other services react to events. No central coordinator. Used in event-driven architecture. Decentralized, but complex to trace and debug. Events published to message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ). Event-driven sagas use choreography.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Orchestration pattern in microservices.
Design Patterns.back: Orchestration: central orchestrator service coordinates workflow. Calls services in sequence/parallel, handles failures, compensates. More control, easier monitoring (state machine). Risk: orchestrator becomes monolith. Workflow engines: Temporal, Camunda, AWS Step Functions. Orchestration-based sagas.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Domain Event pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Domain Event: significant business event captured as first-class object. Raised when something notable happens (OrderPlaced, InvoicePaid). Event handlers trigger side effects (send email, update inventory, publish integration event). DDD tactical pattern. Stored in event store for audit trail.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Value Object pattern (DDD).
Design Patterns.back: Value Object: immutable object defined by attributes (not identity). Equality by value. Examples: Money (amount + currency), Address (street + city + zip), Color (RGB). No ID field. Automatically interchangeable. Python: dataclass(frozen=True), NamedTuple. Persistence: embedded (MongoDB document) vs separate table.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Entity pattern (DDD)?
Design Patterns.back: Entity: object with distinct identity (ID) that persists across changes. Equality by identity. Mutable. Examples: User (user_id), Order (order_id), Product (product_id). Repository pattern stores entities. DDD aggregate: cluster of entities with root entity guarding invariants.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Aggregate pattern (DDD).
Design Patterns.back: Aggregate: cluster of domain objects treated as unit. Aggregate Root: single entry point entity. Clients modify aggregate only through root. Invariants enforced by root. Transactional boundary: entire aggregate loaded/saved atomically. Example: Order aggregate (Order as root with OrderLines). Keep aggregates small.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Repository pattern differ in DDD vs generic?
Design Patterns.back: DDD Repository: collection of aggregates, domain-focused queries, returns domain objects. Generic Repository: CRUD operations on any entity. DDD Repository is per aggregate root, uses Ubiquitous Language. Avoid generic repository (leaky abstraction). Repository + Unit of Work for transaction management.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Unit of Work pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Unit of Work: tracks changes to objects during business transaction. Commits all changes as single transaction. Ensures: all saves succeed or all rollback. SQLAlchemy Session is Unit of Work. Django Transaction.atomic. Closely tied to Repository pattern. New session per request/use case.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Specification pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Specification: business rule expressed as predicate object. Combines using AND/OR/NOT. Reusable, composable. Use: query building, validation, business rule checking. Python: callable classes with __and__, __or__. SQLAlchemy hybrid: criteria + Python check. ORM integration: filter by specification.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Layer Supertype pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Layer Supertype: base class for all objects in layer. Provides common behavior: ID generation, timestamp management, serialization, equality operators. Python: BaseModel (Pydantic), mixins (TimestampMixin, IDMixin). Reduces code duplication, enforces conventions. Used in all layers (domain, persistence, presentation).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Separated Interface pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Separated Interface: define interface in separate package from implementation. Decouples client from implementation. Allows multiple implementations swapped at runtime. Python: ABC in dedicated module. Use: plugin systems, dependency injection, cross-boundary definitions. Interface owned by client.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Registry pattern (DDD).
Design Patterns.back: Registry: global object for looking up references to domain objects. Service locator variation. Types: singleton registry (global), thread-local registry (per-thread), request-scoped. Replaces passing references throughout object graph. Use with caution: hidden dependencies. Prefer DI container over registry.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Factory (DDD) pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: DDD Factory: encapsulates complex aggregate creation logic. Creates valid aggregate with all invariants satisfied. Separates creation from domain logic. Factory method on aggregate root for simple creation. Separate Factory class for complex creation. Ensures aggregates are always in valid state.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Ports and Adapters (Hexagonal) architecture.
Design Patterns.back: Hexagonal architecture: application core (domain) isolated from external systems. Ports: interfaces defining how core communicates externally (inbound/outbound). Adapters: implementations of ports (REST, DB, message queue, UI). Test: swap adapters (in-memory DB, test API). Main: Dependency Inversion Principle.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Onion Architecture?
Design Patterns.back: Onion: concentric layers with dependencies inward. Core: domain model (entities, value objects). Application services: use cases. Infrastructure: persistence, external APIs. Presentation: UI/API. Domain has no dependencies. Everything depends on domain. Dependency inversion: interfaces defined in inner layers.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Clean Architecture.
Design Patterns.back: Clean Architecture (Uncle Bob): entities (enterprise business rules) -> use cases (application business rules) -> interface adapters (controllers, presenters, gateways) -> frameworks (web, DB, UI). Dependency rule: dependencies point inward. Outer layers (DB, framework) are details, swappable.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Service Layer pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Service Layer: defines application boundary with use cases. Coordinates between domain objects, repositories, external services. Implements transactions, authorization. Types: service interface + implementation, or thin service calling domain logic. FastAPI routes call service methods.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Data Mapper vs Active Record trade-offs.
Design Patterns.back: Data Mapper: domain objects don't know DB. Repository maps. More testable (mock repository), pure domain model. More code. Active Record: domain objects handle own persistence (save, delete, find). Faster to implement. Violates SRP. Data Mapper for complex domains. Active Record for simple CRUD apps.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Table Module pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Table Module: single class handles business logic for all rows in table. Multiple instances vs single class. Used with Record Set (DataSet in .NET). Less common in Python. SQLAlchemy: table reflection + dynamic classes. For table-oriented thinking rather than object-oriented.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Transaction Script pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Transaction Script: organizes logic as single procedure per use case. Simple, procedural. Good for simple operations. Becomes unwieldy for complex logic (duplication). Use: simple CRUD, quick implementations. For complex problems: Domain Model pattern preferred.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Domain Model pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Domain Model: rich object model with business logic, invariants, rules. Combines data and behavior. Complex class relationships. Scalable to complex business logic. Requires ORM mapping (Data Mapper). High development effort upfront. Enterprise applications. DDD promotes Domain Model pattern.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Active Record pattern in Python.
Design Patterns.back: Django ORM follows Active Record: model class maps to table, instance maps to row.  Model.save(), Model.objects.get(), model.delete(). Business logic in model methods. Simple, intuitive. Violates SRP (persistence + domain). SQLAlchemy declarative similar to Active Record, but underlying Data Mapper.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Identity Map pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Identity Map: ensures each object loaded only once per transaction. Maintains map of ID -> object. Subsequent loads return same instance (reference equality). Prevents stale data, keeps consistent view. SQLAlchemy Identity Map in Session. Django QuerySet cache serves similar purpose.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Query Object pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Query Object: represents DB query as object. Encapsulates filter criteria, sorting, pagination. Builder pattern for query construction. Python: SQLAlchemy Query object (session.query(...).filter(...).order_by(...)). Separates query construction from execution. Reusable query specifications.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Metadata Mapping pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Metadata Mapping: defines mapping between objects and DB tables in metadata (XML, annotations, dict). ORMs use metadata mapping for column mapping, relationship mapping, inheritance mapping. SQLAlchemy: declarative mapping (Column types, relationships). Hibernate: XML/annotation mapping.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Lazy Load pattern in ORM?
Design Patterns.back: Lazy Load: related objects loaded only when accessed. SQLAlchemy: lazy='select' (separate query on access), lazy='joined' (JOIN in same query), lazy='subquery' (subquery). N+1 problem: avoid lazy loading in loops (use eager loading). Django: select_related (JOIN), prefetch_related (separate query + merge).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Identity Field pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Identity Field: stores DB primary key in object. Pattern for mapping object identity to DB row. Strategies: assigned key, generated key (auto-increment, UUID, sequence). SQLAlchemy: Column(Integer, primary_key=True). Django: AutoField. Surrogate key (auto-increment) vs natural key (business meaning).

Design Patterns.front: How does the Foreign Key Mapping pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Foreign Key Mapping: maps object association to foreign key column. Many-to-one: FK in child table. One-to-many: FK in child with backref. Many-to-many: junction table. SQLAlchemy: relationship('Other', foreign_keys=[...]). Django: ForeignKey, ManyToManyField. Direction of navigation affects mapping.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Association Table Mapping pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Association Table: maps many-to-many relationship via junction table. Separate table with two FKs. SQLAlchemy: Table('association', Base.metadata, Column('left_id', ...), Column('right_id', ...)). Django: ManyToManyField creates join table automatically. Additional columns on association table (order, quantity).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Dependent Mapping pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Dependent Mapping: child object cannot exist without parent. Cascade persistence: save parent cascades to children. SQLAlchemy: cascade='all, delete-orphan'. Delete-orphan: removes children no longer in collection. No separate repository for dependent objects. Value objects mapped as dependent.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Serialized LOB pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Serialized LOB: stores object graph as serialized blob (JSON, pickle, XML) in single column. No join queries, simple schema. Cons: no queryability inside blob, coupling to serialization. Use: value objects, simple data structures, configuration blobs. PostgreSQL JSONB for queryable JSON storage.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Concrete Table Inheritance pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Concrete Table Inheritance: each concrete class has its own table. No shared table. Polymorphic queries across classes impossible (UNION needed). SQLAlchemy: __tablename__ per class, no inheritance mapping. Simpler, no nullable columns. Duplicate columns across tables.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Single Table Inheritance pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Single Table Inheritance: entire class hierarchy in one table. Discriminator column identifies type. Columns for all subclasses (nullable). Simple queries (no joins). Wasted nullable columns. SQLAlchemy: single table inheritance with polymorphic_identity. Django: proxy models (same table, different behavior).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Class Table Inheritance pattern.
Design Patterns.back: Class Table Inheritance: each class in hierarchy has its own table (base + subclasses). Shared columns in base table. Subclass tables have FK to base. JOIN query for full object. SQLAlchemy: joined table inheritance. Django: multi-table inheritance (Parent ptr FK). Good normalization, more complex queries.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Inheritance Mappers pattern work?
Design Patterns.back: Inheritance Mappers: ORM handles loading/saving inheritance hierarchies. Types: single table (one mapper), class table (mapper per class + base), concrete table (mapper per concrete class). Mapper registers subclass discriminators, joins across tables (class table), or union queries (concrete table).

Design Patterns.front: What is the Embedded Value pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Embedded Value: value object stored as columns in same table (not separate). Inline columns: address_street, address_city. No joins. SQLAlchemy: composite column types. PostgreSQL: composite types, document types (JSONB). Embedded vs separate table: queryability, normalization, usage pattern.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Repository pattern for testing.
Design Patterns.back: Repository mock: swap real DB repository with in-memory implementation. Tests run fast, no DB setup. In-memory dict-based repository. Test: CRUD, query methods. Integration test: real repository + test DB. Abstract repository interface enables swapping. Ports and Adapters for testability.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Unit Test pattern for mocking repositories?
Design Patterns.back: Mock repository: use unittest.mock or pytest-mock. Mock returns test data, verify calls made. Avoid over-mocking: integration tests with real DB for query logic. Repository mock: mock_session.query().filter().all.return_value = [...]. Verify: query building, result transformation.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Value Object persistence work?
Design Patterns.back: Embedded: columns in owning table (money_amount, money_currency). Serialized: JSON blob column for complex values. Separate table with FK (address table with FK to person). Trade-offs: queryability, normalization, coupling. Choose based on: query patterns, value complexity, change frequency.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Memento pattern for undo/redo.
Design Patterns.back: Memento: snapshot object state without breaking encapsulation. Originator creates memento with state snapshot. Caretaker stores mementos (stack for undo). Checkpoint/restore pattern. Python: __getstate__/__setstate__ for pickle integration. Use: editor undo, transactional rollback.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Specification pattern for queries?
Design Patterns.back: Specification: reusable criteria object. AND/OR/NOT composition. SQLAlchemy: specification pattern generates filter criteria. Combine for complex queries. Test each specification independently. Example: CustomerIsPremium(), OrderIsShipped(). Specification.And(CustomerIsPremium(), OrderIsShipped()).

Design Patterns.front: Explain the DI Container (IoC Container) pattern.
Design Patterns.back: DI Container: framework that automatically resolves dependencies and injects them. Reads configuration (Python: wiring via modules, Django: AppConfig). Manages object lifetimes: singleton, scoped (per request), transient (new each time). FastAPI Depends, inject (Python DI library), Spring IoC container.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Fluent Interface pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Fluent Interface: method chaining for readable API calls. Each method returns self (or intermediate object). Use: query builders (Query.filter().order_by().limit()), configuration (Builder.withA().withB().build()), assertions. AssertJ, pandas method chaining. Python: return self for fluent API.

Design Patterns.front: Explain the Monostate pattern (Singleton variation).
Design Patterns.back: Monostate: share state across all instances (not single instance). All instances share same class-level __dict__. Python: __shared_state = {} in __init__, self.__dict__ = __shared_state. Multiple instances, same state. More flexible than Singleton (inheritance, transparency). Both have shared global state issues.

Design Patterns.front: What is the Multiton pattern?
Design Patterns.back: Multiton: Singleton per key (enum or string). Registry of Singletons. Python: dict of instances, key-based access. Use: per-thread singletons, per-connection singletons, named services. Class-level dict mapping key -> instance. Thread safety for dict access.

Design Patterns.front: How does the Pool pattern differ from Object Pool?
Design Patterns.back: Pool: general resource reuse (connections, workers, threads). Object Pool: specific pattern for reusable objects with acquire/release. Pool is concept, Object Pool is implementation. Connection pool (SQLAlchemy pool), Thread pool (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). Object Pool is one specific type of pool.
